## **The structure of micelles and microemulsions** 

Yves Chevalier? and Thomas Zembf 

+ Laboratoire des matiriaux organiques, CNRS, **BP 24,** F69390 Vernaison, France $ Dipartement des lasers et de physico-chimie, CEN Saclay, F91191 Gif-sur-Yvette, France 

##### Abstract 

From simple micelles in water, nearly spherical aggregates of amphiphilic molecules, to bicontinuous microemulsions, oil and water microheterogeneous mixtures stabilised by a surfactant film with both local and large-scale disordered structures, the world of surfactant-containing systems is fascinating. Depending on a subtle balance of attractive and repulsive interactions between molecules at interfaces, an extraordinarily rich polymorphism of aggregated structures can be observed. After summarising the basic general constraints controlling surfactant aggregation and the formation of interfaces, different structures of micelles and microemulsions are reviewed and related to interfacial film properties and the intermolecular interactions inside them. With such systems, both static (time-averaged) and dynamic properties control structures equally well. Structures of very different systems can be described in simple ways in terms of surfactant film average curvatures and flexibility. 

This review was received in its present form in April 1989.

**_The structure of micelles and microemulsions_**

#### 1. **Introduction: definition of micelles and microemulsions** 

**A** surfactant molecule contains at least one polar hydrophilic part and at least one apolar hydrophobic unit, such as a hydrocarbon chain. Typical examples are soaps (sodium alkanoates) or phospholipids which form membranes. These molecules may be also called amphiphilic or tensioactive. The coexistence of two opposite types of behaviour (hydrophilic and hydrophobic) inside the same molecule is the origin of local constraints which lead to spontaneous aggregation into microscopic labile structures observed with surfactants in solution in oil or water. 

These supermolecular aggregates, at thermodynamic equilibrium, give surprising macroscopic properties to the solution. They could be explained in terms of microscopic structure by McBain (1913) and Hartley (1936). Knowledge of these structures, their equilibrium, formation and growing conditions is important for detergent manufacture, cosmetic industries, mineral flotation and the understanding of chemistry in heterogeneous media. Micellar aggregation is a primitive but easily controllable model for membranes. Therefore, these structures have been intensively studied in the last ten years; nearly two thousand papers indexed with micelle (or microemulsion) together with the keyword ‘structure’ have been published. 

This review attempts to select the main physical aspects relevant to the surfactant aggregate’s structure, which can be described in terms of mass, volume, shape, oil-water interface, dynamic equilibrium, shape fluctuations, internal molecular packing, etc. It does not cover the thermodynamic aspects and applications, for which we refer to reviews of Tanford (1973, Wennerstriim and Lindman (19794, Lindman and Wennerstrom (1980), Cazabat and Veyssie (1984), Degiorgio and Corti (1985) and Zana (1987), and special symposium proceedings edited by Mittal and others (1977, 1979, 1982, 1984, 1986). 

The simplest possible aggregate is the micelle (sometimes called ‘direct micelle’), which is a cluster of surfactant molecules in water (figure 1). In such a definition, a micellar solution is a dispersion of surfactant molecules in aqueous or apolar solvent with a characteristic size. **A** hypothetical measurement of the mass distribution of the aggregates at a given time would display a maximum for a given range of number of molecules included in a given aggregate at a given instant (figure 2). This number **_Nago_** is called the aggregation number. 

This micellar behaviour has to be distinguished from ordinary molecular solutions in which molecules are individually dispersed in the solvent, solutions of molecules associated as dimers or oligomers produced by stacking of planar molecules. The progressive aggregation (broken curve in figure2) leads to a monotonic decrease of concentration with size in the distribution curve: as concentration is increased, aggregate size varies strongly and no characteristic size independent of concentration can be defined in this case. Such aggregation behaviour is observed with porphyrins or bile salts (Zana **_et_** _al_ 1977), although the origin of aggregation is the same as for micelles (‘hydrophobic bonding’). 

Micellar aggregation can be demonstrated by measurements of physical properties against surfactant concentration. The most significant property is surface (or interfacial) tension (figure **3). As** surfactant concentration is increased, surface tension is

We restrict our discussion to solutions where only short-range interactions exist, the local order does not extend to more than few average sizes of an aggregate. This eliminates the field of lyotropic liquid crystals (mesophases) (Ekwall 1975, Skoulios 1978, Charvolin 1983), where order extends into macroscopic distances, at least in one dimension, leading to Bragg peaks in scattering patterns. Reference to mesophases is, however, frequently made in this paper since it is of interest for comparison between structures occurring in samples having similar compositions. 

The most important property of micellar solutions is their ability to solubilise hydrophobic solutes. In the same way, reverse micelles dissolve water. Once water is solubilised in the micellar core, it is common to use again (but incorrectly) the expression ‘reverse micelle’: this expression should be reserved for binary-binary surfactant-oil mixtures but is widely used in the literature and we will use it too. For direct micelles, solubilisation of an apolar molecule results in ‘mixed micelles’ or ‘swollen micelles’. The ability to dissolve another molecule is called the ‘solubilising power’ of the micellar solution. The first studies of phase diagrams in micellar systems (Ekwall **_et_** _a1_ 1969a) have shown that short-chain alcohols can greatly enhance the solubilising power of the solution: the added alcohol is therefore called ‘cosurfactant’. 

When a large amount of oil is added to a surfactant in solution in a hydrophobic solvent, or when a large amount of water is dissolved in a hydrophobic solution of surfactant, the usual term is o/w (respectively w/o) microemulsion. Since ‘large’ is not a precise definition, there is no difference in nature between micelles with an added solute or swollen micelle and a microemulsion. So far as physics rather than industrial processes is concerned ‘micelles’ and ‘microemulsion’ can be considered as synonyms. 

Once the cosurfactant is added, the solubilising power can become infinite: water can be added in any proportion to **a** solution of reverse micelles (or oil to a solution of direct micelles). Stable and clear quaternary mixtures of water (or brine), oil, surfactant and cosurfactant are called microemulsions (Bellocq **_et_** _al_ 1984, Bourrel and Schechter 1988). Microemulsions are easily obtained with high surfactant contents 

284 **_Y Chevalier and_** _T_ **_Zemb_** 

(about 20%). When low surfactant concentrations are used polyphasic systems are obtained, in which excess water or oil separates in a second (or third) phase (Winsor 1948). **A** typical phase diagram is shown in figure **4:** in the Winsor I (WI) and Winsor I1 (WII) diphasic regions, a microemulsion phase coexists with a phase of excess oil (WI) or water (WII), while the triphasic WIII system consists of a microemulsion in equilibrium with two phases of excess oil and water. According to the hydrophilicity of the surfactant and conditions (ionic strength, cosurfactant content, temperature), all or only some of these polyphasic systems are observed. 

Microemulsions with low surfactant content are much more interesting for application purposes and efficient surfactants or mixtures of surface-active compounds are searched for. Successful formulation of a microemulsion requires knowledge of the physics of surfactant association, specially when ‘stability’ against temperature or salt concentration is needed in industrial applications. 

There is no difference in nature between micelles, reverse micelles and microemulsions: the origin of this nomenclature is due to industrial use, referring to rough chemical composition which can include up to **five** components: the two solvents water and oil, a surfactant, a cosurfactant and salt.

**285** 

The first part of this review will describe the conflicting constraints due to the amphiphilic nature of surfactant molecules. **In** the second part, results of structural studies on binary systems (surfactant-solvent) are discussed. The last two parts deal with ternary and quaternary (or more) systems. This classification according to the number of components is much simpler than qualitative designations of systems as micelles or microemulsions whose precise definitions are still controversial (Danielsson and Lindman 1981, Friberg 1982). 

##### **2. Basic rules** 

Self-association of surfactants results from their hydrophobic character, whereas longrange repulsions between their hydrophilic parts prohibit complete phase separation. Limited aggregation then results from a balance between two opposite forces of different spatial range. These two main contributions to the free energy of micelle formation are large and opposite, small variations are therefore very important and have large structural consequences. **A** very rich structural polymorphism is then expected and indeed experimentally observed. 

Any surfactant aggregate, whether it is a micelle or a microemulsion, is constrained by steric hindrance and the energy cost of mixing oil and water. We first discuss these general constraints. **As** a consequence of this balance between two large and opposite forces, segregation of hydrophobic and hydrophilic parts is quite complete, hydrophobic regions being free of hydrophilic parts of molecules. This is quantitatively measured by the transfer energy from water to oil. All geometric constraints described in the following are a consequence of that: constant density, limit of sphericity and the molecular packing criterion. 

##### _2.1. Transfer energy from_ **_water_** _to_ oil 

From their solubility in water (McAuliffe 1966), the free energy of transfer of linear hydrocarbons from water to oil (hydrocarbon) was estimated. This free energy does not depend much on the oil used. From additivity rules (valid for linear hydrocarbons only), the free energy increments per group are -3.7 kJ mol-' for CHI and -8.8 kJ mol-' for CH3 (Tanford 1973, Abraham 1979). They are **-3.2kJmol-'** for **CH2** and -7.3 kJ mol-' for CH3 for the transfer of hydrocarbons from water to micelles, and about -3.0 kJ mol-' for the transfer of CH2 of surfactant from water to micelles. All these values compare well, differences being attributable to hydrocarbon-water contact occurring at the micellar surface. They are also very large, and total segregation of hydrocarbon and water is therefore expected. The similarity of transfers from water to oil and to micelles is a strong indication of a water-free hydrocarbon core in micelles. This is also clear when looking a: the free energy of transfer of water molecules from hydrocarbon to bulk as estimated from water's minute solubility in hydrocarbons (less than 100 ppm (Schatzberg 1963)). 

##### _2.2. Constant density, molecular volumes_ 

The important consequence of the combination of long-range attractive van der Waals and short-range repulsive excluded volume intermolecular interactions is that the density of liquids is constant, even over a few molecular distances. Local departures 

**_Y Chevalier and_** _T_ **_Zemb_** 

286 

from this behaviour can be considered as defects such as in the solid state and are energetically costly. On this basis, molecular volumes in liquids are the same whatever the structure, unless strong interactions occur (hydrogen bonding). They depend slightly on the solvent: getting an alkyl chain out of water into hydrocarbon results in an increase of its volume of the order of 10% (Davies and Bury 1930, Hoiland 1976, Desnoyers et **_al_** 1979, 1980, 1982). These volumes are easily obtained from density measurements or found in tables. 

Tables should be used with caution, volumes taken from crystallographic data, representative of the solid state, should be considered with a 10% uncertainty, since they are underestimates for solutions (Shinoda and Soda 1963). Volumes calculated from densities of pure liquids do not account for solvent effects. Tables of molecular volumes or volume increments per group are available for aqueous solutions (Miller0 1971, Cabani **_et_** al19Sl), and can be used in tandem with an experimental determination of molecular volume, which can be obtained using precise density measurements. Some useful molecular and group volumes are given in table 1. The volumes of the CH, and CH, groups compare well with those of pure hydrocarbons (Huggins 1941, Doolittle 1951). 

The constant density of the micellar core is a constraint that is to be introduced in interpretation of experiments. In theoretical calculations about hydrocarbon packing in micelles, the introduction of the rule of constant internal density is a considerable simplification sime it reduces the number of possible conformations of packed chains. However, Bothorel **_er al_** (1974) and Belle and Bothorel (1974) introduced van der Waals attraction and excluded volume effects through a Lennard-Jones potential, constant density was thus not explicitly stated but was a consequence of these potentials.

##### **_2.3. TanfordS limit of a sphere, surfactant parameter_** _v/a,l,_ 

Surfactant headgroups are always located at the water-hydrocarbon interface, but some water-hydrocarbon contact remains and cannot be avoided. **A** typical case is sodium dodecylsulphate (SDS) as estimated from the comparison of area per headgroup at a micellar interface (60 A'lmolecule) and for SDS diluted in a cholesterol monolayer at the air-water interface (27.5 A2/molecule (Pethica 1955)). Complete coverage by headgroups would require a close proximity between them which is incompatible with their mutual repulsion. Because of its minimum area for a given volume, the spherical shape is the best way to minimise this contact area. Micelles are thus expected to be spherical whenever it is sterically possible. To avoid this water-hydrocarbon contact, water is expelled from the micellar core which is composed of dry hydrocarbon of constant density. In order to fill the whole core volume, at least one methyl group has to be present at its centre and, for headgroups to be at the surface, the micellar radius cannot exceed the maximum length of a surfactant molecule. Tartar (1955) and Tanford (1972, 1973) have shown that spherical micelles can grow up to **a** maximum value of aggregation number **Nsph,** any further growth inducing a shape deformation (figure **_5 ) ._** This limit is calculated on purely geometrical grounds since the volume **_v_** and the maximum length 1, of a linear alkyl chain of **_n_** carbon atoms are:

Indeed, most o f a sphere volume sits close to its surface (a radius increase of 26% doubles the volume). Gruen and De Lacey (1984) have pointed out that a methyl-size hole at the micellar centre is a possible alternative to deformation. The radius increase is 2.35A7 which results in an increase of **Nsph** from 56 to 82 for a hydrophobic chain with 12 carbon atoms. The energy cost is the vaporisation enthalpy of a methyl and is weak (==60 J mol-'). The same geometrical arguments apply to any defined aggregate shape. #### **3. Principles of methods of investigation** 

Each structural method works on a characteristic spatial or time domain. The resolution is an important quantity to be known before any interpretation. The spatial (or temporal) resolution is the smallest distance (or time interval) that can be separated with a given method. Smaller details are smoothed out. 

The structure, as studied by any physical method, is thus smoothed, all the inhomogeneities of smaller size than the resolution being left out. It is therefore not meaningful to introduce overinformative details in a structural model: given a method and its resolution, a suitable model for the interpretation has to be chosen (figure 7). In the following, methods are discussed, starting from the lowest resolution (macroscopic methods) and ending with N M R which works on a molecular spatial domain. **A** gap in experimental methods exists between direct visualisation (optical microscope) which works on a 100 p m scale and light scattering (1 pm). This is currently being filled with video-enhanced microscopy (Evans _et a1_ 1985); direct images of supraaggregate structures are observed which opens a new field of structural investigation (Miller _et a1_ 1987a, b). Since electron microscopy requires freezing and drying of the sample, this technique has not yet been widely used to investigate micelle and microemulsion structure. Transmission electron microscopy, however, can in principle go down to the resolution needed to observe typical scale 10 nm of the size of surfactant aggregates. Freeze fracture electron microscopy (Dubochet _et a1_ 1984, Talmon 1986) has been questioned due to artefacts produced during the shadowing and replication procedures. **A** new technique, known as direct imaging ( DI), has recently proven to

be extremely powerful and, instead of being disturbed by artefacts, the DI technique makes use of the artefacts to distinguish between water and oil domains (Jahn and Strey 1988). Since DI has, independently of neutron scattering, been able to make a clear distinction between connected and disconnected droplets, it is likely that wide use will be made of this technique in structural studies in the future. 

Methods of investigation for dynamical properties are also discussed, taking into account spatial resolution, going from motions of the aggregates, of molecules in the aggregates and of atoms in the molecules. It is restricted to some experimental methods which are the most powerful, general and mainly the most direct, thus reliable ones. A more complete compilation of experimental methods can be found in recent reviews (Wennerstrom and Lindman 1979a, Zana 1987, Kahlweit _er_ **_ai_** 1987). 

#### _3.1. Macroscopic techniques_ 

Because of the characteristic size of heterogeneities, all these methods suffer from a lack of spatial resolution. They are very useful for the observation of transitions, as an abrupt variation of macroscopic properties necessarily reveals some change in microscopic structure. For example, critical micelle concentrations are measured by a large number of macroscopic techniques (Mukerjee and Mysels 1971). The transition from small to large micelles is accompanied by a significant increase in viscosity (Ekwall and Holmberg 1965, Ekwall _er al_ 1971, Nagarajan _et a1_ 1982, Porte and Appell 1984) and the appearance of anisotropic susceptibilities (Hoffmann _et a1_ 1981a, b, c, Porte _er_ **_a2_** 1984). The percolation thresholds are easily observed from macroscopic transport measurements (Lagues _er al_ 1978, Lagues 1979, Lagues and Sauterey 1980, Lagourette _et al_ 1979, Dvolaitzky _er al_ 1980, Zana _et al_ 1982, Clausse and Heil 1983, Cazabat _et al_ 1984a, b). Some macroscopic methods, as applied to structural studies, are briefly discussed in the following. 

One of the earlier methods used in colloid science is viscosity (McBain 1913). This method is still frequently used in polymer science. Intrinsic viscosity [ **771,** obtained by an extrapolation to infinite dilution, is related to the specific volume _V,,_ by [.I] = _a_ **Vsp,** _a_ being a form factor. The particle is defined as the content of a hydrodynamic volume which includes the colloidal particle and all its bound species (condensed counter-ions and hydration water). Because of the large penetration of solvent into the particle, intrinsic viscosity can be used to determine the mass of polymers in solution. This is not the case for micelles. When the size, shape and fraction of bound counter-ions of the particle are already known from other independent determinations, hydration numbers can be obtained. The method seems to work since reasonable values are found, but important problems do exist. The form factor is well established only for spherical particles and its value _a_ = 2.5 is valid under stick boundary conditions at the surface (a = 1 with slip conditions). Accounting for slip, stick or intermediate conditions can be attempted (Altenberger _et a1_ 1985). 

Electrical conductivity and ion activity can be used when ions are present, i.e. with ionic surfactants. Their measurement as a function of concentration provides a measure of the fraction of bound ions. Indeed, the mobility (thus electrical conductivity) of ions is reduced as they bind to an aggregate of low mobility (Evans 1956, Kimizuka and Satake 1962, Satake _er a1_ 1963, Zana 1980, Lianos and Zana 1983). Activity of ions is less, too, when they are embedded in an aggregate, their chemical potential being less than for their free state (BotrC _et al_ 1959, Satake _er a1_ 1969, Sasaki _et_ **_a1_** 1975, Gaboriaud _er al_ 1984, Sepulveda and Cortbs 1985). For the interpretation of 

**_The structure of micelles_** and **_microemulsions_** 

29 1 

these measurements, drastic simplifications are usually made, as shown in figure 8. The results are then strongly dependent on the way the experiment is interpreted and cannot be considered as reliable when used alone, only variations along series are significant. Moreover, the fraction of bound counter-ions depends on the cut-off distance (see $4.1.7) which arbitrarily separates bound and free ions. This separation is decided very clearly in theoretical calculations. On the contrary, the way the instrument proceeds on microscopic distances for making such a discrimination is not known. The result is thus an effective quantity: it accounts for the effect through the way in which it is interpreted; it is not a mean value as would be expected for a macroscopic method. These considerations explain why there is such a large scatter in ‘experimental’ values of bound counter-ion fractions (Sepulveda and _Cortbs_ 1985). Of greater significance are measurements of surfactant activity. The two-states model (free or micellar) is clear and the concentration of free surfactant is determined (Sasaki _et_ all975, Cutler **_er_** _al_ 1978, Vikingstad 1979). For ionic surfactants above their CMC, the concentration of free surfactant is shown to decrease with total concentration, which is in disagreement with the widely used pseudo-phase model. 

Birefringence measurements are useful in studying anisotropic structures. Macroscopically permanent birefringence occurs with lyotropic mesophases which are ordered on large scales. Anisotropy in electric (Rouvibre **_era/_** 1979a, b, Hoffmann **_et_** a1 1981a, b, Schorr and Hoffmann 1981, Neeson _et_ a1 1983, GuCring and Cazabat 1983) or magnetic susceptibility (Meyer _et_ a1 1982, Porte **_et al_** 1984, Rosenblatt and Zolty 1985) or rheological properties (Backus and Scheraga 1951, Scheraga and Backus 1951, Lob1 **_er_** a1 1984, Hirsch **_et_** _al_ 1984a) detects microscopic anisotropies that are averaged out in the absence of an external field. If these effects cannot be ascribed to molecules themselves (Hoffmann and Schorr 1985) or to critical fluctuations (Cant6 **_et_** _a1_ 1985), they are due to aggregates. Apart from this easy way to detect anisotropic structures, these effects can be used to align samples on a macroscopic scale, a useful technique being to perform scattering (Thurn **_et_** a1 1984, Hayter and Penfold 1984, Cummins et

##### _3.3. N M R relaxation methods_ 

Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) is a basic tool for investigating geometric and dynamic properties at a molecular level. Any non-zero nuclear spin can be observed (Brivard and Granger **1981).** When spectral lines do not overlap, each atom can be observed individually. This technique thus has the highest spatial resolution. This obvious advantage has some drawbacks: lower-resolution information such as particle size, although present, is difficult to extract from such abundant information. NMR methods should then be used for structure refinement, when some lower-resolution data are already known. The latter should then be introduced as a constraint for the interpretation. Lastly, obvious constraints should not be forgotten: atoms are tied to one another by chemical bonds of known length and angles, and only few dihedral angles are allowed defining the trans and gauche conformations. Because of spectral resolution problems, studies on ’H N M R are limited, **I3C** or ’H (from specific deuteration) are preferred for hydrocarbon chains studies, and headgroups or counter-ions can be observed by their relevant nucleus. 

296 _Y Chevalier and T Zemb_ 

For quantitative structural studies, two main methods are available: vicinal spinspin coupling constants which are conformation dependent, and relaxation which allows both spatial and dynamic studies. Thus, in this latter case, structural studies depend on an implicit dynamical model. The former has been rarely used because of the want of good spectral resolution. Conformational analysis **has** been only performed near headgroups by means of 'H-IH (Menger and Jerkunica 1977, Maitra and Eicke 1981, Maitra _et a1_ 1983, Ueno and Kisimoto 1983) or other vicinal coupling constants (Belai'd and Chachaty 1984, Chevalier and Chachaty 1984, Faure _et a1_ 1985, Menger and Carnahan 1986, Menger _et a1_ 1987). 

NMR relaxation is due to the modulation of magnetic interactions by rotational Brownian motion, providing geometrical and dynamic (correlation times **7,)** information. The modulation of the magnetic energy is characterised by an autocorrelation function _G( t )_ whose Fourier transformation is the spectral density _J ( w )_ of motion (figure 11). NMR relaxation times are combinations of spectral densities at relevant Larmor frequencies (Abragam 1961). Spin-lattice relaxation ( _T,)_ is thus important when molecular motions occur in the Larmor frequency range. Slow motions having correlation times larger than the inverse Larmor frequency are inefficient in inducing relaxation. Experiments can be carried out at different Larmor frequencies to measure motions on different time scales and are complementary. Very low frequencies **(kHz)** are accessible by rotating frame relaxation **(TIP).** Spin-spin relaxations ( **_T2)_** probe very slow motions through _J(0)._ The highest available magnetic field with commercial NMR spectrometers (14.1 T) sets the upper limit of the N M R frequency domain at 5 GHz. Detailed studies of fast molecular motions would require a factor of the order of ten more. 

Motions in heterogeneous media can be separated into two parts: slow motions of the structure itself and internal fast motions of molecules. Each part corresponds to a different time scale and these motions are uncorrelated; the autocorrelation function is thus a sum of two independent autocorrelation functions pertaining to these motions. This idea, introduced by Charvolin and Rigny (1973) and developed for micellar systems by Wennerstrom _et al_ (1974, 1979), is a two-step application of the general spectral density for a time hierarchy of **_N_** motions which reduce order parameters by successive geometrical increments Si (Davis **_et_** _a1_ 1978, Paddy _et a1_ 1981, Dufourc and Smith 1986) (figure 11):

Quadrupolar relaxation can also be interpreted in the same way (Henriksson _et al_ 1977a). This model is simple, and experiments at three Larmor frequencies allow the determination of the three parameters _T ~_ Tcf _~_ and _,_ S. The slow motion includes the rotation of the micelle and the diffusion of the surfactant molecule at its spherical surface (Alexandre _et a1_ 1973). Studies of anisotropic slow motions are possible (Soderman _et a1_ 1985b). The anisotropy of fast motions is accounted for by S only, their rate ( _T , ~ )_ is assumed to be the same for any orientation (Halle and Wennerstrom 1981). This simplification may seem unrealistic since methylene motions in alkyl chains occur by discrete jumps between trans and gauche positions (van Gunsteren _er a1_ 1981, Jorgensen _et a1_ 1984). It takes advantage of the fact that fast motions do not enter the frequency dependence of _T,_ to model them as simply as possible, but to what extent the model for fast motions influences the other parameters in a fitting procedure is still a question. 

Another problem is the possibility for cross-correlation effects to be important with such anisotropic motions (Hubbard 1969,1970, Werbelow and Grant 1977). Although equilibrium recovery curves were always observed as monoexponential, their systematic inspection seems judicious. The development of more refined spectroscopic methods using these cross-correlation effects (Vold and Vold 1978) is promising for the detailed study of fast local motions (Prestegard and Grant 1978, Fuson and Prestegard 1983, Brown _et a1_ 1985). 

###### **_3.4._** _Raman and infrared spectroscopies_ 

Vibration frequencies of molecular bonds and angles are measured by these techniques. The spatial and time resolutions are very high, to such an extent that these methods are not very sensitive to the environment of the molecule. Raman and I R spectra are intrinsic characteristics of molecules. Given a molecular conformation, they are identical in gas, liquid, solution and solid states unless a specific interaction occurs 

**_Y_** _Chevalier and T Zemb_ 

298 

(solvation, hydrogen bonding, etc). Spectral differences reveal changes in molecular conformation and Raman and IR spectroscopies have mainly been used for conformational analysis of hydrocarbon chains of surfactants. The vibration frequencies being much larger than the rate of conformational isomerisation, the spectra are sums of subspectra of all the conformers present in the sample, the complete information is thus contained in the spectra. Nevertheless, few and essentially qualitative conclusions have been drawn from both these techniques. The reason for this is the large number of conformations and the extremely small frequency differences between the conformer subspectra (Mizushima and Simanouti 1949, Snyder 1967, Snyder _e? al_ 1982). Broad composite bands are then observed which can only be characterised by the frequency of their maximum and their band width. Raman C-C and C-H stretching bands contain lines corresponding to the all-trans conformation (easily assigned with spectra of dry crystalline samples), and additional bands which are assigned as gauchecontaining conformations (Lippert and Petitcolas 1972, Okabayashi _e? al_ 1974, 1975, 1982, Kalyanasundaram and Thomas 1976, Rosenholm _et al_ 1976, 1977, Burns _e? a1_ 1982, Amorim da Costa and Santos 1983, Brooker 1984). 

IR spectroscopy became possible with the important sensitivity enhancement brought about by the introduction of Fourier transform IR spectroscopy, allowing the study of aqueous solutions. Only shifts of band maxima could be observed (Umemura **_et_** _a1_ 1980, 1981, Kawai _e? a1_ 1984) and, like Raman spectroscopy, only relative variations over different samples can be studied. Another limitation is the sensitivity; the solutions must be fairly concentrated and, if the influence of micellisation is to be studied, spectra should be recorded below the CMC. Most studies then deal with short chain surfactants which have large CMC and pre-aggregates are observed below the CMC, making the observation of unassociated molecules difficult. The main conclusions of these studies are the expected results: the micellar core is liquid-like (gauche conformations are present) and the probability of all-trans conformation is larger in micelles than for monomeric molecules and increases with concentration (as the area per headgroup decreases). The combined use of these two spectroscopic techniques, together with the use of deuterated compounds (Rosenholm _et al_ 1976), could lead to more quantitative results, if improvements in sensitivity (Kamogawa _et a1_ 1984) are achieved. When surfactant molecules contain a function which has some isolated band (a double bond, the pclar head, etc) (Okabayashi **_et_** _al_ 1982, Okabayashi and Abe 1980, Okabayashi and Matsushita 1984, Umemura _e? al_ 1980, 1981, Cameron _et al_ 1982, Brooker 1984, Kawai _et a1_ 1984) clearer conclusions can be drawn. 

##### _3.5. Methods involving the use of probes_ 

The methods previously described make use of intrinsic probes. X-ray or neutron scattering use only intrinsic electron or scattering length, NMR uses non-zero nuclear spins. Some techniques such as electron spin resonance (ESR), fluorescence, uv or visible absorption are not so general. Most organic molecules (especially surfactants) do not contain unpaired electrons nor absorb light. When the medium has not itself the necessary spectroscopic property to enable such experiments to be performed, it can be introduced into the medium by means of added molecules called probes. The addition of the foreign molecule is assumed not to perturb the structure under study, but it is generally not possible to ensure that this is actually the case. These methods are then only useful to back up known results, or conclusions which need to be confirmed by more reliable methods. Nevertheless, they should not be completely 

_The structure of micelles and microemulsions_ 

299 

rejected as they may allow useful complementary experiments to be carried out on known structures: as an example, dynamic fluorescence or **ESR** can work on time domains below the time resolution of NMR. 

Generally, the interpretation of such experiments is dubious because, for unique experimental data, two important factors are unknown: the structure under study and the localisation of the probe in this structure. The incorrect use of such probe methods had led to an incorrect model of micelles (Menger 1979, 1984). Thus, because added hydrophobic probes have the same spectroscopic properties as in polar solvents, it was concluded that water should penetrate the micellar core (where probes were assumed to sit) (Kalyanasundaram and Thomas 1977, Menger _eta1_ 1978,1981, Menger 1979, Menger and Boyer 1980, Menger and Bonicamp 1981, Menger and Chow 1983, Menger and Doll 1984, Martens and Verhoeven 1981, Turro and Okubo 1981, Russell and Whitten 1982). An alternative (and correct) interpretation is that these probes solubilise in the interface (Wennerstrom and Lindman 1979b, Zachariasse **_et_** _a1_ 1981, 1984, Ganesh _et a1_ 1982, 1984). Probes are also used to monitor the ‘local’ or ‘effective’ polarity oftheir solubilising site (Mukerjee _et a1_ 1977, Donchi _et_ **_a1_** 1980, Zachariasse _et a2_ 1981, 1984). Such quantities have never been clearly defined and reference to macroscopic dielectric constants is generally made. Since heterogeneities have molecular dimensions, descriptions by means of macroscopic quantities defined from statistical physics are forbidden. The meaning of such experiments is thus obscure and their practical use questionable. 

**A** classical example is the determination of the so-called microviscosity or fluidity by studying the motions of probes. Once the structure is known, probe motions reflect internal motions of the host, provided that dimensions of the solvent compartment are large enough for edge effects to be neglected and for reference to bulk solvent to be significant. The problem of localisation of the probe remains and requires an independent determination, although it is frequently neglected. When solutes solubilise at the interface, experiments have to be interpreted at a molecular level (Aoudia _et a1_ 1984a, b). Hydrophobic cores were found to be as fluid as bulk alkanes (Singer 1982, Shinitzky _et a1_ 1971, Pownall and Smith 1973, Kalyanasundaram _er a1_ 1975, Zachariasse 1978, Emert _et a1_ 1979, Turro _et a1_ 1979, Turro and Okubo 1981, Stilbs _et a1_ 1983a). Cores of water-in-oil microemulsions could also be studied with water-soluble probes but their adsorption at the polar interface cannot be excluded (Wong _et a1_ 1976, 1977, Valeur and Keh 1979, Keh and Valeur 1981). 

###### **4. Binary micelles** 

###### _4.1. Micelles in water_ 

Sometimes called ‘direct micelles’, binary micelles in water are obtained by spontaneous dissolution of surfactant. They have to be distinguished from vesicle solutions which are usually obtained as clear solutions upon dispersion with high-power ultrasound (sonication), i.e. addition of mechanical energy to produce a state which is metastable for most surfactant molecules tested so far. 

_4.1.1. Current theoretical models of micellar structure._ It is now accepted that dilute micellar aggregates are spherical droplets of aggregated surfactant molecules: the first direct proof has been obtained by Reiss-Husson and Luzzati (1964) by comparing the x-ray scattering spectra on an absolute scale with lamellar and spherical geometries. 

##### **_Y Chevalier and_** _T_ **_Zemb_** 

Before this crucial work, it was accepted that small-angle scattering had ‘proved’ that micellar solutions were a dilute dispersion of surfactant bilayers of the same nature as surfactant vesicles. This ’proof’ was only supported by the similarity of shape between scattering spectra of bilayers and micelles. 

Micellar aggregation occurs because two opposite contributions to the free energy of micellisation are present. The task of thermodynamic models is to calculate the standard chemical potential _po( N )_ of a surfactant molecule in a micelle of aggregation number _N._ The size distribution is directly obtained and properties are deduced from the relevant partial derivatives of the free energy. These are to be compared with experimental structural data. **_pug(_** _N )_ may include many terms according to the degree of sophistication of the model. The main difficulty is to describe the mutual repulsions of headgroups in the interface which include electrostatic interactions at a molecular level (a dielectric constant cannot be defined), steric hindrance, solvation, etc. **A** complete thermodynamic theory of micellar aggregation would be of enormous intricacy and consequently rather obscure, the few main contributions have been examined by several authors. Some known structural information has necessarily been introduced into models and a single term in _p O ( N )_ expressions often includes several physically distinct phenomena. Tanford ( 1974a, by 1977) has considered hydrophobic and interfacial free energies and was able to calculate with some success the free energy for different sizes and shapes; the area per headgroup was related to the micellar size and shape by simple geometrical considerations since the micellar core is water free. The hydrophobic contribution was obtained from the known free energy of transfer of a surfactant molecule from water to hydrocarbon corrected for water-hydrocarbon contact at the interface (which is equivalent to adding an interfacial tension term). The interfacial free energy proportional to the inverse area per headgroup was taken from experimental pressure-area isotherms at water-hydrocarbon interfaces. The problem is that the high curvature of micelles is not accounted for by pressure-area data which concern flat interfaces. Israelachvili er **_al_** (1976, 1980) and Mitchell and Ninham (1981) calculated curvature contribution by modelling the interface as a curved capacitor. This model, which retains the same area per headgroup dependence as Tanford’s, is especially valid for zwitterionic or ionic surfactants at high ionic strength for a complete electrical neutralisation of the interface to occur at small distances. 

An alternative is to calculate the electrostatic free energy by a numerical resolution of the Poisson Boltzmann equation in a cell (see § 4.1.7) (Gunnarsson **_et_** _al_ 1980). Upon addition of a rough estimate of the free energy of chain packing inside the micellar core as a third term and rotational and translational entropy, McMullen er **_a1_** (1984a, b) have shown that many aggregate shapes are allowed and may be in equilibrium because of their small energy differences, so that a defined shape cannot be **_a priori_** decided for a model. Extreme refinement of chemical potentials is insignificant compared with the basic assumptions of such theories. Indeed, all these calculations work with chemical potentials varying as the logarithm of mole fractions, thus under ideal solution conditions. This is obviously a formally incorrect assumption as interactions must be present for aggregation to occur, a problem which has been addressed by Mitchell and Ninham (1981). The important feature in thermodynamic theories is the cancellation of large and opposite contributions which makes the system very sensitive to slight changes in external conditions. 

Very different and contradictory models for micellar structure have been proposed, and the discrimination between them has occurred only recently (figure 12). The original oil droplet model is due to Hartley (1936): micelles are spherical with a liquid 

**_The structure of micelles and microemulsions_** 

**301** 

**Figure 12.** Different structural models of micelles as they have appeared in the literature. **_( a )_** Hartley (1936) spherical micelle with a disordered, water-free, hydrophobic core; _( b )_ Hartley micelle as used for the interpretation of scattering experiments; (c) Menger (1979) micelle with extensive water penetration in the core; **_( d )_** Fromherz (1981a, b) surfactant block model with maximum order inside the core; **_( e )_** Dill (1984a, b) and Cantor (1984) model for filling the micellar core with hydrocarbon chains, no chain folding is allowed; _(f)_ Gruen (1985a, b) model of chain packing inside the micellar core is the result of simple constraints (consrant inner density, headgroups sitting at a spherical interface). 

water-free core made of hydrocarbon chains; headgroups are at the interface. This model is still used for the resolution of scattering experiments, an outside 'interfacial' layer contains the headgroups, bound counter-ions and hydration water. Two contrasting models of internal structure have appeared: Menger (1979) proposed a loose micelle with a large penetration of water inside its core. The extensive water-hydrocarbon contact allows the interpretation of spectroscopic and reactivity experiments using probes (see **0** 3.5). In contrast, Gruen (1985a, b) proposed a model similar to Hartley's in that the micellar core is liquid and water free, and has calculated hydrocarbon chain packing at constant density inside it. Dill and Flory (1980, 1981), Dill and Cantor (1984), Dill (1984) and Cantor and Dill (1984) have presented similar calculations, but the surfactant alkyl chains were not allowed to fold. From the idea that the internal state of micelles is intermediary between that of a liquid droplet of uncorrelated alkane molecules and that of a crystalline lamellar phase, Fromherz (1981a, b, 1984) builds **up** a micelle with preformed trimers of parallel correlated surfactant molecules. 

**302** _Y Chevalier and_ **_T Zemb_** 

Dimensions of a trimer block are expected to correspond to the correlation length of molecules within the block. Micelles are built with perpendicular blocks up to the aggregation number and a well defined cubic shape results from this model. 

**_4.1.2._** _Aggregation number, volume and average shape._ Aggregation numbers are measured by means of scattering methods (see B3.2). This way is more direct than many other methods described in the literature and is free of any choice of thermodynamic model. The main feature of experimental results is that micelles are either small, their size being 1 to 1.5 times the maximum possible size of a perfect smooth sphere, or very large. Small micelles are obtained with ionic and zwitterionic surfactants, while large ones are made up with non-ionics or ionics under conditions of high ionic strength (Chen 1986a, b). This is consistent with the idea that size is controlled by repulsive interactions between headgroups at the interface. When repulsions increase, the surfactant parameter _a&/ U_ increases and micelles get smaller. 

**As** a consequence, size and CMC are related: surfactants with low CMC aggregate into large micelles, the higher the CMC, the smaller the micelles. Experimental evidence which supports this picture is size variations upon changing interfacial electrical charge. Thus, a continuous size increase (and CMC decrease) is observed as salt is added in ionic micellar solution (Emerson and Holzer 1967, Hayashi and Ikeda 1980, Bendedouch _er a1_ 1983a, b, Hayter and Penfold 1983, Cabos 1983, Imae and Ikeda 1985). The same effect is obtained when the surfactant solution is concentrated, increasing the ionic strength (Hayter and Zemb 1982, Hayter and Penfold 1983, Zemb _er a1_ 1983, Bendedouch _er a1_ 1983a, b, Magid _er a1_ 1983, Drifford **_et_** _a1_ 1984, Berr _et al_ 1986b, Sheu _er a1_ 1987). Salt does not actually change the electrical charge per headgroup but screens interheadgroup repulsions upon condensation effects. **A** true headgroup charge variation can be obtained with derivatives of weak acids (carboxylates, phosphates, etc): lowering the pH causes protonation of some anionic headgroups with a subsequent charge variation. A similar effect can be obtained by complexation with charged species such as calcium cations (Trauble and Eibl 1974, Tocanne _et a1_ 1974, Verkleij er _a1_ 1974). Alkylcarboxylic acids are water insoluble (infinite aggregation) while the corresponding carboxylates form small micelles. Corkill _et a1_ (1970) and Ikeda _et al_ (1979) have shown a size decrease as a zwitterionic surfactant is converted into a cationic one. 

Chevalier _er a1_ (1985) allowed the charge of alkylphosphates to vary from one as in conventional surfactants to two. Highly charged micelles are found to be small and polydisperse, their size showing a strong concentration dependence. The size of monocharged surfactant micelles exceeds slightly the limit of sphericity and depends only slightly on concentration. Some general trends can be outlined from available experimental data. Short-chain or highly charged surfactants form spherical polydisperse micelles whose size is lower than the limit of sphericity (figure 13). Long-chain (above about eight carbon atoms in a linear chain) monocharged surfactant micelles reach quickly a plateau in their size dependence with concentration (figure 14). Micelles are slightly aspherical (Cabane _er a1_ 1984, 1985, Berr _er a1_ 1986a) and further growth is hindered. Size increase implies a strong deformation and occurs abruptly as a sharp transition (improperly called second CMC), giving rise to the very large micelles discussed in the next section. 

Non-spherical micelles should be expected whenever the radius of a sphere, including the measured number of surfactant molecules, exceeds the length of the fully extended surfactant molecule.

**_4.1.3. Large micelles._** The area per headgroup in an ellipsoid being less than that of a sphere, the transition to large micelles occurs upon a reduction of interheadgroup repulsions. **It** may then be caused by salt or surfactant addition, or solute solubilisation (such as alcohols (Ekwall er **_a1_** 1969a)). Difficulties in experimental studies of such either concentrated or ternary solutions have been overcome in early work by a crude modelling as rigid cylinders without mutual interactions (Mazer **_et_** _a2_ 1976,1977, Missel **_et_** _al_ 1980, 1982, 1983). If most conclusions cannot resist a careful reinterpretation, the small enthalpy difference between spheres and cylinders has been recognised and measured (Mazer and Olofsson 1982). Micellar growth is then controlled by entropy and a large polydispersity is expected. 

Because of the limited length of a surfactant molecule, at least one dimension of large aggregates is equal to twice this length, leading to cylinders with spherical end caps or lamellae with toroidal rims. Such aggregates may be flexible. Energetically unfavourable edges can be avoided upon formation of toroids from cylinders or vesicles from lamellae, but the energy reduction may be compensated by a decrease of deformation entropy. Porte (1983) has shown that toroids are unlikely because of their bending entropy, but that vesicles should occur in those conditions. 

Anisotropic aggregates are easily detected by induced birefringence or depolarised light scattering measurements. Most structural investigations of these systems are quasielastic light scattering studies. Intermicellar structure factors as well as hydrodynamic interactions (Ackerson 1978) are generally ignored. 

**In** this case, attractive interactions could be misinterpreted as micellar growth. Such interactions occur with nonionic surfactant systems but may also occur in ionic ones (see 94.1.7) (Appell and Porte 1983, Bendedouch and Chen 1984, Chao **_et_** _a1_ 1985). On the other hand, the experimental autocorrelation functions obtained from light scattering are not single exponentials. Biexponential decays corresponding to overall translational motion and internal structure fluctuations have been observed as varying the scattering angle (Flamberg and Pecora 1984, Pecora 1984). Most experimental evidence is then only of qualitative significance, if shear does not induce structural perturbations, shear alignment should allow more reliable conclusions to be made, aggregate dimensions and flexibility being observed (Cummins **_et_** _a1_ 1987a). As salt is added, rod-like micelles are formed which become flexible as they grow further (Porte **_et_** _a1_ 1980, Porte and Appell 1981, Appell and Porte 1981, Appell **_et_** _a1_ 1982, 

305 

_The_ **_structure_** _of micelles and microemulsions_ 

Hoffmann _er a1_ 1983, Imae and Ikeda 1984a, b Imae _er a1_ 1985, van de Sande and Persoons 1985). 

The transition from rigid to flexible micelles as well as the persistence length of coiled micelles depends on the nature of the surfactant molecules. 

Indeed, the strength of interfacial interactions governs the variation of area per headgroup and thus the flexibility. When flexibility is strongly hindered as in hexadecylpyridinium salicylate micelles, interacting rigid rods are observed, resulting in a visoelastic behaviour of the solution (Gravsholt 1976, Ulmius _er aJ_ 1979, Hoffmann _et al_ 1981a, Kalus _et_ **_al_** 1982, Lob1 **_et_** _a1_ 1984). Micellar growth is limited and a size decrease is observed at high concentrations; flexibility is nevertheless achieved with high enough electrolyte concentrations (Hoffmann **_et_** _a1_ 1981b, 1983 Angel _et a1_ 1984). 

This behaviour is reminiscent of that of polymers: a rod-to-coil transition is observed while adding salt into a polyelectrolyte solution (Drifford **_et_** _al_ 1985), a coiled polymer in a good solvent changes its conformation suddenly into a rod as a non-solvent is added (Lim _et a2_ 1983). Candau _et al_ (1984,1985) have noticed that the behaviour of large micelles as monitored by light scattering follows the same scaling laws as semidilute polymer solutions (Tmae and Ikeda 1986, Kat0 _et_ **_al_** 1987). With such an analogy, the description of micellar solutions as a dispersion of interacting particles is abandoned for a network of flexible rods correlated over a characteristic length **_6_** (figure 15). 

**Figure 15.** Schematic diagrams of large flexible micelles (left) and their semidilute solution with a rough definition of the correlation length (right). 

As a micellar solution is concentrated, micelles grow in size and ordered mesophases made up with infinite aggregates occur. In certain cases, the micellar size may remain finite and anisotropic micelles (large to small axis ratio <3 (Charvolin er _a1_ 1979, 1984, Hendrikx _et a1_ 1983)) get ordered in concentrated solutions, giving rise to nematic mesophases (Lawson and Flautt 1967, Rosevear 1968, Radley _et a1_ 1976, Fujiwara er all979, Fujiwara and Reeves 1980, Forrest **_et_** _a1_ 1980, Forrest and Reeves 1981, Gelbart _et al_ 1985). With nematic phases, some continuity exists between micellar solutions and infinite aggregates in mesophases (figure 16). The incomplete powder average due to macroscopic ordering allows more structural information to be obtained out of experiments. Internal segregation in multicomponent micelles could be demonstrated in this way, the small headgroup compound being concentrated in the low-curvature

_4.1.4. Hydration, water penetration in the micellar core interface thickness._ Water is the surrounding medium of direct micelles and some water molecules are bound to the hydrophilic groups at the surface. The dehydration of the interface is necessary for two micellar cores to merge and requires the dehydration energy. Hydration water is thus defined as belonging to the hard volume of the micelles and is of importance for their stability. 

The definition of hydration numbers requires the splitting of water into two physically distinct states as bound and free, which may seem arbitrary. Hydration of the interface first occurs through hydrogen bonds of high energy. If two micelles come into contact and coalesce, hydration water has to be removed. Hydration water 

**_The_** _structure_ **_of micelles_** _and_ **_microemulsions_** 

307 

participates in the stabilisation of aggregates. The definition of hydration is thus the number of water molecules which are not expelled when micelles come into contact. This is also the definition currently used for protein structure studies (Tardieu **_et_** _al_ **1987).** The case of micellar colloids is simpler, since, in contrast to proteins, only one type of hydration water exists (water cannot enter hydrophobic regions). 

Different definitions have been previously used, mainly for technical reasons: early studies of hydration made use of volume differences between dry particles (from static scattering methods) and hydrated ones (from dynamic measurements), hydration water **is** then that which moves with the particle in a two-state model. It was shown that these two different hydration numbers are frequently identical, but it should be recognised that all surfactant molecules studied so far were quite similar, differences could occur for chemically different headgroups. Several other hydration processes may occur: especially water structuring near hydrophobic regions (Badiali 1985, Tarazona and Vicente 1985). This phenomenon has been demonstrated by measurement of direct forces between mica plates (Pashley and israelachvili 1984, Israelachvili 1985) (figure 17). It should not be inferred that unbound water is completely free. In ionic micellar solutions, electric fields are present everywhere in the solution and, because of the high dielectric constant of water, orientation of water molecules occurs everywhere.

Between water and hydrocarbon, the region of mixing is called the 'interface'. The interface is therefore defined as the region where neither water nor hydrocarbon may be considered as free of the other component. The interface thickness is related to the interfacial tension. 

**_Y_** _Chevalier and T Zemb_ 

308 

It should be noted that the interfacial area depends strongly on its localisation for systems with high curvature (with _v/aol,_ very different from one). This problem is difficult with direct micellar systems of high curvature and the choice of a clear definition for the interface should be provided every time an area per headgroup value is put forward. 

According to this definition of the interface, each type of hydrophilic group has a well defined hydration number. These numbers are usually obtained by comparing the micelle hydrodynamic volume with its dry volume (Kushner and Hubbard 1954, Mukerjee 1964, Courchene 1964, Ekwall and Holmberg 1965, Schott 1967) or by self-diffusion measurements of water (Lindman and Brun 1973, Lindman _et_ **_al_** 1976, 1980a, b). It is then assumed that only strongly bound water moves with micelles (two-site model). **A** more direct way, according to the above definition, is to evaluate the hard volume through interaction measurements (Hayter and Zemb 1982, Chevalier _et_ **_al_** 1985). **In** cases of ionic micelles with strong condensation of counter-ions, the hard volume may be as large as twice the dry volume. 

It was inferred that water could enter very deeply into the micellar core, forming ‘fjords’ in it (Menger 1979). This erroneous conclusion was based on incorrect interpretation of experiments involving the use of added probes (see **0** 3.5). The absence of water inside the micellar core has been clearly demonstrated by NMRrelaxation (Clemett 1970, **Pod0** **_et_** _al_ 1973) and small-angle neutron scattering (Cabane _er_ **_al_** 1984, 1985) experiments. Some water-hydrocarbon contact occurs, however, as headgroups are not bulky enough to allow a complete coverage of the hydrocarbon. The first methylene of hydrocarbon chains is also exposed to water because of its fast protrusive motion out of the micelles. 

For this contact area to be a minimum, the interface has to be smooth, as observed by small-angle neutron scattering: the interface thickness is less than the experimental resolution (5A) (Tabony 1984, Cabane _et_ **_al_** 1985). This picture agrees with the small compressibility of micellar interfaces (Bloor _et al_ 1984). 

**_4.1.5._** _Fluctuations_ **_of_** _the interface._ Small micelles have an average spherical shape. This picture comes from experimental measurements which provide averages. Monte Carlo calculations allow simulations of the structure of an isolated micelle and have shown considerable shape fluctuations (Haan and Pratt 198 1, Owenson and Pratt 1984, Pratt _et_ **_al_** 1986). The time (or number) average is spherical. The width of the distribution of radii (distances between headgroups and centre of mass) is as large as the average radius. Headgroups remain, however, fully exposed to water. This wide distribution is entirely due to shape fluctuations and is neither an average interface thickness nor a water penetration into the micellar core. **On** the contrary, Ljunggren and Eriksson (1984) have shown that these large fluctuations occur only when the interfacial tension is low. 

Fluctuations from a spherical shape require an area increase which is limited by interfacial tension. When the interfacial energy is less than **_kT,_** large fluctuations are allowed, which is not the case for micelles **_( U_** = 15 mM m-I). Monte Carlo calculations provide larger shape fluctuations but the model is rough. The resolution of these calculations is only one third the length of a hydrocarbon chain. The chain flexibility is restricted by the lattice spacing, so that possibilities for a spherical micelle to occur are few. Conclusions should be confirmed through a more refined model and experiments. Shape fluctuations have been proposed for the interpretation of small-angle neutron scattering experiments with **’H** labelled surfactants (Cabane _et_ **_al_** 1985) (see 

**3** 09 

_The_ **_structure of micelles and microemulsions_** 

**P** 4.1.6 and figure 19). The best theoretical simulations available are compatible with these experimental results (Haan and Pratt 1981, Halle **er** _al_ 1988). 

Some neutron spin-echo inelastic scattering experiments (Hayter and Penfold 1983, Huang et _a1_ 1987) allowed a direct measurement of the contribution of the shape fluctuations of the interface. 

**_4.1.6. Packing of hydrocarbon chains._** Hydrocarbon chains are confined in a medium of defined average shape and have to fill its whole volume with a constant density. The micellar core being liquid-like (Roberts and Chachaty 1973) and free of water (see **48** 2.1 and 4.1.4) its density is that of a liquid alkane. Headgroups have, moreover, to sit at the interface. Gauche conformations have an energy 2.3 kJ higher than trans ones (Flory 1969). The alkyl chains must obey these three constraints. 

Both experimental and theoretical approaches have been used in studying this problem. Theoretical ones consist in calculations of the free energy of all the conformations which satisfy these three constraints (Bothorel **_er a1_** 1974, Belle and Bothorel 1974, Gruen 1981, 1985a, **by** Gruen and De Lacey 1984, Ben-Shad er **_a1_** 1984, 1985, Ben-Shad and Gelbart 1985, Szleifer **_er a1_** 1985). **A** different approach from Dill and Flory (1980, 1981), Dill and Cantor (1984) and Cantor and Dill (1984) suffers from the inability of chains to fold; further, it disagrees with experimental observations of the occurrence of terminal methyl groups at the interface. 

Current theoretical studies assume that micelles are only spherical on the time average, significant instantaneous deviation being possible and headgroups being located at the surface, and that the internal core is ‘liquid’. They show a great disorder in the micellar core, in agreement with its liquid-like character. The orientational order is larger for the first methylenes (close to the headgroups) than at the end of the alkyl chains. Chains were also found uncorrelated (Gruen 1985a), which seems surprising allowing for the constraints and since correlations do exist in bulk liquid alkanes (Bothorel 1968, 1974, Bothorel **_et_** _a1_ 1972, Fourche and Bothorel 1969). This orientational order can be estimated through an order pzrameter S = (3 cos? 19-1)/2, **_I9_** being the angle between the radial vector and the normal to the H-C-H plane of a methylene (Edholm 1982). This order parameter is twice that found by **I3C** N M R relaxation (see **3** 3.3) and allows successful comparisons with experimental data (Gruen 1985a, b) (figure 18).

Experimental determination of the order parameter along the chain shows a very slight dependence of the order parameter profile on area per headgroup (Mily _er al_ 1975, Charvolin and Hendrikx 1985). 

The radial distribution of methylenes has been studied by small-angle neutron scattering and does not fully agree with chain packing calculations. Bendedouch _er_ **_al_** (1983a) have deduced a distribution of terminal methyl groups which peaks towards the micelle centre. This is a result of the poor experimental resolution. A more disordered picture emerges from high-resolution experiments (Cabane _et a1_ 1985) which show broader distributions than theory (figure 19). Packing calculations agree with molecular dynamics (van der Ploeg and Berendsen 1983) and Monte Carlo (Haile and O’Connell 1984) simulations carried out under similar hypotheses, namely a well defined aggregate shape. This discrepancy could be ascribed to shape fluctuations which have not been introduced into theoretical models. When some fluctuations in the headgroup positions are allowed, the group’s distributions indeed broaden in the correct way (Woods _et a1_ 1986). The internal structure models are thus essentialiy correct but the choice of one particular (average) shape for the micelle introduces too much order into the structure. Further progress in this field requires more structural data to be introduced in the model, namely shape anisotropy and fluctuations as discussed in § 4.1.5.

_4.1.7. Efectit.e charge, bound counter-ions, interactions between ionic micelles._ The structural charge of a micelle (molecular charge times aggregation number) is considerably reduced by counter-ion condensation, especially when large concentrations of salt are added. This leads to a smaller charge, as experienced far from the micelle (from another micelle). This net charge, reduced by counter-ions ‘near’ the interface, is referred to as ‘effective’ charge. 

It is therefore usual to classify counter-ions as bound and free (see § 2.6), which is a good approximation when compared with the resolution of most experimental techniques (Clifford and Pethica 1964, Lindman and Brun 1973, Lindman _et a1_ 1976, 1982, 1984a,b Kamenka _er a1_ 1974, 1977, Smith 1979, Stilbs and Lindman 1981, Almgren _et al_ 1985, Lindstrom _er a1_ 1985, Jansson and Stilbs 1985). 

**_The structure of micelles and microemulsions_** 

311 

‘Bound’ counter-ions are only electrically attracted toward the micellar surface, there is no real chemical binding and counter-ions remain fully hydrated (Gustavsson and Lindman 1975, Lindman **_et_** _a1_ 1976). 

With ionic surfactants, a highly charged polyion should result from aggregation of hydrophobic ions. Counter-ions of opposite charge are then attracted toward the micelle as in any polyelectrolyte solution. This counter-ion ‘condensation’ contributes to micelle formation, their presence close to the charged interface reduces its charge density and makes the aggregate stable by weakening electrostatic repulsions between headgroups. It is usual to separate counter-ions into two states as condensed (or bound) and free, and a fraction of bound counter-ions **_a_** is defined. For scattering studies, a counter-ion is considered to be ‘bound’ if it is included in the excluded ‘hard sphere’ volume of the aggregate. It turns out to be nearly equivalent to the definition of the **_f_** potential, where the ions are bound when they move with the Brownian motion of the particle. The ‘bound’ state is therefore much more general than a chemical binding. 

The radial concentration profile of heavy counter-ions can be studied in the wide-angle region of small-angle x-ray scattering patterns. The very high resolution of NMR is of no help because of the fast exchange rates of ions between different environments. Bound counter-ions allow charged headgroups to get close to each other, providing the micellar aggregate with its stability. They thus belong to the micelle. Removing counter-ions from the surface causes an increase of area per headgroup. Increasing the charge of headgroups causes more counter-ions to condense. 

Given an ion, compensation occurs when one attempts to modify the effective interface charge, for example by pH variation around the pK of the headgroups, so that the effective charge per unit area is kept constant around a reasonable value of some p C cm-’ for a given _aoZ,/u_ (Chevalier **_et_** _a1_ 1985, Drifford **_et_** _a1_ 1985). Intermicellar interactions are repulsive with monovalent counter-ions and the micelles are stable. The potential between ionic micelles is, in all cases studied so far, well approximated as the sum of a hard sphere and screened Coulomb potentials, even if the real potential is obviously more complicated (Cabos **_et_** _al_ 1979, Corti and Degiorgio 1981, Hayter and Penfold 1981a, b, 1983, Hayter and Zemb 1982, Magid **_et_** _al_ 1983, Triolo **_et a1_** 1983, Bendedouch and Chen 1983, 1984, Cabane **_et_** _a1_ 1984, 1985). 

As salt is added, or with multivalent counter-ions, the strong intermicellar correlations become vanishingly small. For high ionic strengths, the electrostatic repulsive potential is weakened to such an extent that an attractive van der Waals potential may predominate (Bendedouch and Chen 1984, Chao **_et_** _a1_ 1985) and demixing phenomena are observed (Appell and Porte 1983). This DLvo-type description should be modified: because of counter-ion size and correlations, electrostatic interactions can be attractive. 

Looking at counter-ions as point-like electrical charges only is an oversimplification. Counter-ions have their own specificity. Although it may not be the only important factor, the size of hydrated ions strongly influences the micellar behaviour. Given a charge, hydrophobic (less hydrated) counter-ions show larger condensation effects (Marra 1986) and give rise to a smaller area per headgroup. Thus, hexadecyltrimethylammonium or hexadecylpyridinium bromides aggregate into large micelles which turn into hexagonal mesophases when concentrated, while chlorides form spherical micelles which get ordered as cubic mesophases (Anacker and Ghose 1968, Ulmius **_et_** _al_ 1978, Almgren **_et_** _a1_ 1979, Porte **_et_** _a1_ 1980, Porte and Appell 1984). With cations, the differences are less (Mukerjee **_er_** _al_ 1967, Cabos 1983, Berr **_et a1_** 1986a), however, complexation of cations with a cryptand results in a considerable growth of counter-ion 

312 **_Y_** _Chevalier_ **_and T_** _Zemb_ 

size and a concomitant reduction of micellar size (Evans _er a1_ 1986b, Miller _er_ **_al_** 1987a, b). Highly hydrated hydroxide counter-ions are adsorbed far from the interface on cationic micelles, which are consequently small (Lianos and Lang 1983, Hashimoto **_er_** _a1_ 1983). The same occurs with organic counter-ions, but their behaviour is more difficult to rationalise (Jansson and Stilbs 1985, 1987). The viscoelastic behaviour of hexadecyltrimethylammonium salicylate micellar solutions is also due to the specific high condensation of the counter-ion (Ulmius _er a1_ 1979, Hoffmann _er a1_ 1981a, b, 1983, Kalus **_et_** _a1_ 1982, Lob1 _er_ **_a1_** 1984, Angel **_et_** _a1_ 1984, Olsson _et al_ 1986). Upon a photochemical transformation of the counter-ion, Wolff and von Bunau (1984a, b, 1986), Wolff _er a1_ (1987) and Muller _er_ **_a1_** (1984) drastically change the macroscopic properties of micellar solutions. Studies with hydroxide or organic counter-ions have shown the limits of conventional theories of micellar aggregation (primitive models of electrostatics): spontaneous vesicles are formed (Ninham _et a1_ 1983b, c, Talmon _et a1_ 1983, Hashimoto **er** _a1_ 1983, Brady _et_ aZ1984, 1986) and vesicle-to-micelle transitions can be observed. This suggests that some unknown additional interactions which are usually neglected become important (Evans _et a!_ 1986a, Ninham and Evans 1986). 

The electrical potential of the aggregate, although screened by counter-ion ‘condensation’, is efficient over large distances. The larger the ionic strength (surfactant and added electrolyte concentrations), the smaller its range. **In** direct micelles, the screened electrostatic potential between two colloidal droplets is therefore a valid approximation (Hayter and Penfold 1981a, b): 


![](10.1088_0034-4885_53_3_002_assets/Y_Chevalier_1990_Rep._Prog._Phys._53_279-f84e8a69d0.pdf-0035-03.png)


This electric potential applies for two rigid spheres of charge _Zo_ and diameter _a._ separated by a continuous medium where counter-ions are considered as point-like and the ionic strength fixes the inverse Debye length **_K._** As a rule of thumb, the inverse Debye length (in angstroms) in pure water at 25 _“C_ is given by **_K_** = 0.33&, c being the ionic strength expressed in moles per litre. 

This potential applies only outside of the hard sphere ‘core’, which includes the ‘bound’ counter-ions and the hydration water. It can be shown that this one-component macrofluid ( OCM) approach is formally equivalent to the more rigorous calculation of pair distribution functions between micelles using HNC (the hypernetted chain, see below) to solve the ‘primitive model’ where no ‘bound’ counter-ions exist since all counter-ions are taken into account with their own diameter in this two-component model (Belloni 1986a). 

The counter-ions are distributed in water according to their electrostatic energy. The counter-ion distribution is given by the Poisson-Boltzmann equation. This equation has no analytical solution, and different types of approximations are used in order to solve it analytically or numerically. The most reasonable compromises between approximations and computational heaviness are Poisson-Boltzmann cell numerical methods (Marcus 1955, Alexandrowicz 1962, Alexandrowicz and Katchalsky 1963, Katchalsky _er a1_ 1966, Bell and Dunning 1970, Westra and Leyte 1979, Delville 1980, 1984, Delville _er a1_ 1984, Gunnarsson _et a1_ 1980, 1982, Bratko and Vlachy 1982, Belloni _er a1_ 1984). In these procedures, the solution is modelled as an electroneutral cell containing one aggregate of uniform charge density immersed in a continuous solvent where point-like ions sit. The cell volume is the inverse number density of monodisperse aggregates and has the same symmetry as the aggregates. **As** ions are assumed point-like and influenced by the polyion screened potential, ion-ion correlations are neglected.

This method compares well with numerical simulations (Monte Carlo, Brownian dynamics (Linse **_et_** _a1_ 1982, Akesson and Jonsson 1985)) for monovalent counter-ions and low charge densities. It may be unsuccessful, however, in accounting for intermicellar properties (osmotic pressure) because micelle-micelle correlations are not considered in a cell model (Wennerstrom **_et_** _a1_ 1982, Linse and Jonsson 1983, Jonsson **_et_** _a1_ 1984). 

In the case of failure, some more accurate models are available such as the hypernetted chain (HNC) (Elkoubi **_et a1_** 1977, Rogers 1980, Beresford-Smith and Chan 1982, Linse and Jonsson 1983, Kjellander and Marcelja 1984, Belloni 1985). Theoretical calculations usually show different kinds of counter-ions as going away from the charged surface which can be separated into two classes, ‘condensed’ and ‘free’ (figure 20), once a clear definition of the boundary has been adopted, giving significance to the two-state model for ions.

Because of ion-ion correlations (counter-ion excluded volume effect) and interface electrical polarisation, deviations from Poisson- Boltzmann behaviour may be considerable (Nagele _et a1_ 1985). Indeed, because of the mobility of amphiphilic molecules at a dielectric discontinuity, the hypothesis of uniform charge density at the interface no longer applies when charged counter-ions (especially multivalent ones) approach it; a surface polarisation occurs which can be easily accounted for by the introduction of fictitious image charges in electrostatic calculations (Kjellander and Marcelja 1985a). Depending on the location of surface charges about the dielectric discontinuity, attraction or depletion of counter-ions results from the image charge phenomenon (Kjellander and Marcelja 1984, 1985b, Linse 1986, Bratko _et a1_ 1980). On the other hand, because of ion-ion correlations with bulky, multivalent counter-ions, the electrostatic attraction of micelles by counter-ions may exceed the intermicellar repulsion when it is weakened enough by counter-ion screening (far enough from the charged micellar surface). An intermicellar attraction is then found which is electrostatic in origin and can be considered as a condensation of micelles around counter-ions (Muller and Derjaguin 1983, Guldbrand _et al_ 1984, Svensson and Jonsson 1984, Kjellander and Marcelja 1985a, b, 1986a, b, Belloni 1986b). 

_4.1.8. Attraction between micelles: cloud points and phase equilibria._ Dispersion forces between identical particles are always present and attractive, so that attractive interactions between micelles always occur. Such interactions may also have different origins. Electrostatics are so important and long range with ionic systems, that they allow attractive interactions to be neglected, except when high salinity (0.1 mol 1-’ screens electrostatics at distances shorter than the average intermicellar distance, leaving the van der Waals attractions as the main interaction). Also, this is not the case for non-ionic surfactant systems. These surfactants are of wide industrial use and the most studied molecules are polyoxyethylene alkylethers of general chemical formula H(CH2),T(0CH2CH2),0H often abbreviated as C,EO,. **As** attractive interactions become important, the solution becomes cloudy (turbid) and demixing occurs: the

Closed diphasic domains showing both behaviours are sometimes observed (Herrmann _er a1_ 1966, Lang and Morgan 1980, Lang 1984) (figure 22). Critical points are always present. Note that an upper consolute boundary in water and simultaneous lower consolute boundary in oil explains the full ternary phase diagram of non-ionic microemulsions (Kahlweit _et a1_ 1988). 

Phase diagrams have been put into a unified picture and explained through simple geometrical arguments by Mitchell _e? al_ (1983). An interesting feature of these binary systems is that, depending on compounds, the direct (L,) and reverse (LJ micellar domains are either separated by a lamellar mesophase domain or form a unique monophasic domain in the phase diagram. In this latter case (figure23), surfactant and water can be mixed in any proportion. However, it does not account for the possible ‘melting’ of lamellar phases into reverse micelles, the L2 phase is thus not predicted. The structure of this **L2** phase is not known. 

In the dilute region, where structure is the simplest to study, the non-ionic micelles are generally small at the CMC **(Nags L-** 80-200). 

Considerable growth may occur, depending on compounds, even for fairly dilute solutions.
