_4.1.9. Dynamic aspects: Brownian motion and molecular exchange._ Because of their small size and internal liquid-like character, very fast dynamic processes occur in micellar solutions. They are numerous according to the time or spatial scale considered. They are split into several different types, mainly because experimental methods work for a given time and spatial resolution and are only sensitive to some of these motions. At low resolution, translational and rotational motions of the micellar entities occur. **On** a smaller scale, motions of surfactant molecules in micelles are observed: exchange of molecules between solvent and micelles, surface translational diffusion, molecular rotational motion. Next, rotational intramolecular motions (gauche-trans isomerisations) are considered. Time scales are related to the spatial extent of motions as they are for all Brownian motions: energy is the same **_(kT),_** so that small-amplitude motions are fast. Translational diffusion of micelles is studied by means of quasielastic light scattering (QELS), pulsed field gradient spin-echo NMR (PFGSE) (Stilbs 1987) or diffusion of radioactive tracers (Kamenka _et a1_ 1984). QELS provides mutual diffusion constants which are equal to self-diffusion constants at the CMC when intermicellar interactions vanish (Pusey 1978), i.e. at infinite dilution of aggregates. The latter are directly obtained from PFGSE or tracer diffusion (Nilsson _et a1_ 1983, Nilsson and Lindman 1983, 1984). **A** method based on polarography has been also used for self-diffusion measurements (Zana and Mackay 1986). Self-diffusion constants are related to the hydrodynamic radius of the micelles through Stokes-Einstein relations, and to obstruction by other micelles (Jonsson _et a1_ 1986). This is a powerful means of measuring micellar size as a function of concentration. The size is that of the hydrated micelle. Mutual diffusion constants depend, moreover, on intermicellar static and hydrodynamic interactions. QELS as a function of scattering vector and selfdiffusion measurements provides a set of complementary data (Pusey 1978) which allows a complete description of dynamic structure when a correct model for static interactions is used. 

Exchange of surfactant molecules between water and micelles used to be studied with chemical relaxation methods (temperature or pressure jumps, fast mixing by stopped flow) or ultrasonic relaxation. The current theoretical description of these processes is due to Aniansson _et a1_ (1976) with some further refinements (Almgren _et al_ 1977a, by Lessner _et a1_ 1981a, by Wall and Aniansson 1980, Elvingson and Wall 1986). Two relaxation processes are observed (Lang _et a1_ 1975). The fast one is molecular exchange at a constant fraction of micellised molecules and the second one is due to variations of this fraction through micelle formation or breakdown (figure 25). The rate constants of entrance of surfactant molecules into micelles is always the same **_(k+_** = lo9 mol-' s-I) (Aniansson _er a1_ 1976, Hoffmann _etaZ1981d),_ which suggests a diffusion-controlled process. The exit rate **_( k - )_** is strongly dependent on the alkyl chain length and only weakly on the nature of headgroups (anionic, cationic or non-ionic). The variation of **k-/Na,,** with chain length gives an energy barrier per methylene equal to the free energy of micellisation (the equilibrium constant **_K_** = exp(hG/RT) is equal to **_Na,,k+/k-);_** it follows the CMC variations (Aniansson _et a1_ 1976, Hoffmann 1978). 

The diffusion of surfactant molecules at the interface is a two-dimensional process (headgroups remain at the interface). The diffusion constants as measured in lamellar mesophases by PFGSE are of the order of lo-'' to lo-'' m2 _s-'_ (Charvolin and Rigny

Molecular and intramolecular rotations are difficult to separate experimentally. They occur on time scales of comparable magnitude and are certainly correlated. Most N M R theories assume uncorrelated motions, which is their main limitation. These motions are restricted in amplitude and anisotropic because of packing constraints in the micellar core. The approach of Wennerstrom et _a1_ (1979) is the most realistic one in spite of some approximations (anisotropic motions are assumed to be isotropic in rate and uncorrelated). 

Motions of the same type and time scale are combined together, so that the full spectral density is described with only three parameters: a slow motion correlation time _T,,,_ a fast one **_rCf_** and an order parameter _S_ which characterises the anisotropy of fast internal motions (see 03.3) (Ahlnas et _a1_ 1983, 1984, Lindman **er** _a1_ 1983, Walderhaug et _a1_ 1984, Soderman et _a1_ 1985a, b, StCbt er _a1_ 1985, Ntry et _a1_ 1986, Eriksson er _al_ 1987). Slow-motion correlation times are in the nanosecond range as discussed above, their decrease with micellar radius fully agrees with this interpretation (Soderman et _a1_ 1987). Fast movements are in the picosecond range; similar but a little bit slower than in liquid alkanes, and they do not depend on aggregate size. The weak dependence of _r,,_ on the position of the carbon atom in the alkyl chain is **a** strong indication for occurrence of correlations between internal motions whatever

The consequence of such agreement is that no motion slower than 1 GHz influences molecular orientation in either micelles or mesophases. 

##### **_4.2._** _True reverse micelles: micelles_ **_in_** _organic apolar solvents_ 

True reverse (or inverted) micellar solutions are binary solutions made up with surfactant and an organic apolar solvent, i.e. without any water. The micellar core is then made of polar headgroups. Hydrophobic chains are directed towards the solvent. 

There is some controversy about the possibility of surfactants aggregating without any water or polar impurity (Eicke and Christen 1978). It seems nevertheless that such cases may occur, since the amount of impurities should be important for one molecule to be present in each micellar core. Some surfactants do not aggregate without added water (Becher 1960, Kitahara 1965, Guveli 1984), but the great majority do (Elworthy 1959, Becher 1960, Kitahara _et a1_ 1962, Fowkes 1962, Eicke and Christen 1974, Eicke and Rehak 1976, Zulauf and Eicke 1979, Tavernier _et a1_ 1981, Sudholter and Engberts 1982, Ravey _et_ **_al_** 1984, Ravey and Buzier 1984, Guveli 1984). 

In spite of its chemical instability and difficulties of purification (Fletcher **_et al_** 1984, Delord and Larch6 1984), the most popular surfactant is sodium di2-ethylhexylsulfosuccinate or Aerosol OT **(AOT)** for its low cost, its ability to solubilise large amounts of water at room temperature and the important available experimental studies. Structural data dealing with true reverse micelles are few, attention being focused on ternary systems containing water. Many non-ionic surfactants are of poor purity, and techniques which provide number average aggregation numbers (vapour pressure lowering, membrane osmometry, vapour pressure osmometry) have often been misinterpreted. Measurements by these techniques have to be extrapolated down to infinite dilution (to the CMC) in order to obtain interaction-free structural data. On this basis, the general belief that true reverse micelles are only oligomers (dimers, trimers, etc) is unsound. Claims of concentration-independent aggregation numbers and of large differences between number average and mass average aggregation numbers from light scattering indicating polydispersity (Sirianni _et a1_ 1962) seem dubious. These two statements are, moreover, contradictory since polydisperse micelles necessarily have concentration-dependent aggregation numbers (see § 4.1.2). In this field, general reviews should then be read with caution (Eicke 1980). 

Some general trends can, however, be outlined. Although it is not always the case, a CMC above which micellar aggregation occurs can be defined and measured. The CMC can be rather high (Ravey **_et_** _al_ 1984, Ravey and Buzier 1984). Below the CMC, surfactant molecules associate into oligomers, and rather large micelles can exist above it (Elworthy 1959, Tavernier _et a1_ 1981, Kumar _et_ **_a2_** 1984, Kotlarchyk _et a1_ 1985) and are in equilibrium with sub-cMc small aggregates (Eicke _et a1_ 1975). Aggregates should be called micelles only when aggregation numbers are enough (at least 10) for a deep minimum in the size distribution to be possible. The absence of size variation with 

**_The structure of micelles and microemulsions_** 

**321** 

concentration was observed by Huang **_er_** _a1_ (1984), as well as the occurrence of an attractive intermicellar potential. 

**In** the absence of water, self-association of water molecules cannot be the origin of aggregation, and true reverse micelles are in that way different from those containing water in their core. Headgroups are dipoles, especially ionic ones that exist as ion pairs in apolar solvents. Electrostatic dipole-dipole attraction between headgroups should then be important and long range because of the low dielectric constant of the surrounding solvent, and considered as the driving force for aggregation. Association of two dipoles into a dimer results in a quadrupole of lower energy and so on. The situation is similar to ion cluster formation in polymer ionomers (Eisenberg 1970, Yarusso and Cooper 1983, Dreyfus 1985), the unfavourable elastic energy of the polymer chain being replaced by entropy of mixing. A larger aggregation is possible but limited by entropy and interfacial interactions which determine the curvature. Hydrocarbon chain-solvent interactions are of importance in these latter interactions (Eicke and Christen 1974, Eicke 1979). Thus, Little and Singleterry (1964) and Little (1970) related the micellar size of dinonylnaphthalene sulfonates to the solvent solubility parameter _6_ of Hildebrand. Such interactions are short range as concentration does not affect the structure. Dynamics of surfactant molecules are similar to those of direct micelles (Faure **_et‘_** _al_ 1987). 

The main interest of reverse micelles is their ability to dissolve water in their core, forming water-in-oil microemulsions as discussed below. 

##### **_5._ Ternary systems** 

Phase diagrams of ternary systems are more complex than those of binary systems. Figure **_26_** is a typical example, illustrated by the hexadecylammonium bromide-waterhexanol system (Ekwall **_et_** _al_ 1969a). At high water content, the direct micellar phase **L1** and in the oil corner, the ‘reverse micelle’ or ‘water-in-oil’ microemulsion are the two isotropic phases. Between them, the usual liquid crystalline mesophases occur, in this case the lamellar and hexagonal phases. 

The picture which emerges from the micellar structure of binary solutions of surfactants and water (L,) is the following: a fluctuating oil droplet with a smooth interface is built by the hydrocarbon tails. The interface contains charged headgroups with a huge amount of water (typically ten molecules per headgroup) included in the micellar ‘hard sphere’ excluded volume: when two micelles come into contact, this water volume is not expelled. The residence time scale of a molecule in a given aggregate is in the nanosecond range, probably the same as the shape fluctuations. How does this picture change when a third component is added? 

Additional components can be classified into several classes: 

(i) With short-chain alcohols as third component, the solubility of oils in micellar solutions is greatly enhanced: alcohols are called ‘cosurfactants’. The extreme case where all the surfactant is replaced by alcohol, leaving **a** clear and stable ternary mixture of oil, water and alcohol without any surfactant (‘detergentless microemulsions’) is beyond the scope of our survey of surfactant systems (Smith **_er a1_** 1977). **A** complete analysis of phase diagrams and related Surface tensions has been made by Puig **_et_** _al_ (1987). 

(ii) Of practical interest in detergency applications is the case where the third component is insoluble in the pure main solvent (solubilisation). Apolar molecules

On the other hand, water can be solubilised in a binary mixture of oil and surfactants. **In** most cases, the solubilising power towards a third component is low: the solubilisation limit of hydrocarbons is of the order of one to five solute molecules per surfactant. 

(iii) Some exceptions to this low-solubilisation limit are known: the cases of **AOT** for anionic amphiphiles, of nonylphenol polyethyleneoxide for non-ionic surfactants (Marsden and McBain 1948) and of double-chain cationic ammonium surfactants such, as didodecyldimethylammonium bromide ( **DDAB)** (Fontell **_er al_** 1986). 

(iv) Another ternary system is the ‘mixed micelle’, where a mixture of surfactants is used in water. This is a very active field because of industrial applications: a synergic effect in solubilising power is expected, since the surfactant shape parameter **_a,l,/v_** can be adjusted at will with the chemical composition of the surfactant mixture. 

Although studies on solubilisation behaviour in surfactant systems are numerous, reliable results in a system under good control are few, mainly because of the lack of phase diagram determination. Two classical reference works giving complete phase diagrams in ternary surfactant systems are due to the Swedish group (Ekwall **_et a1_** 1969a, b). Solubilisation by a surfactant solution occurs below the CMC: a hydrophobic molecule can induce micellar nucleation. The effect of a foreign substance on a binary solution is shown to increase the thermal stability and the domains of existence of the micellar phases. The work of Ekwall’s group is also a critical review of most of the ternary phase diagrams known ten years ago. 

The case of added salt is somewhat different: we consider a mixture of salt, water and surfactant as a binary system, since the main effect of the salt is to screen out the electrostatic interactions between ionic headgroups; surfactant, salt and water mixtures are therefore described in § **4.** 

_The structure of micelles and microemulsions_ 

323 

##### **_5.1._** _Models of structure_ 

The situation for ternary systems is more complicated than for binary systems: when a model of spherical interacting droplets breaks down, i.e. when an autocoherent iterative fitting procedure does not work, one has to invoke locally lamellar, rod-like or disc-like structures. This is geometrically possible because of local segregation of the components in a mixed aggregate: alcohols, which have a lower _aol,/u_ parameter than surfactants, tend to accumulate in the cylindrical regions rather than at the highly curved parts of the ellipsoid like swollen micelles: this effect has been directly observed by neutron scattering using deuterium-labelled molecules (Hendrikx _et_ **_al_** 1984). 

Unfortunately, the scattered intensities for these structures cannot be calculated analytically. One has either to neglect interactions between particles, an assumption which cannot be right in real systems (even at very low concentration of the order of 1% volume fraction, interactions between aggregates are important). On the other hand, one could consider only the power law behaviour of the scattered intensities, but this procedure can be very misleading. The only path is to calculate numerically the scattering of the proposed structure on an absolute scale (Barnes and Zemb 1988). This is the main reason why most published results in ternary systems use some kind of spherical droplet model with an interaction potential. On the other hand, this quite simple assumption has been claimed to hold surprisingly well for some surfactants such as **_AOT_** (Kotlarchyk 1984) (figure 32). 

If the microstructure is a collection of spherical droplets, the basic rule is simple: since the area per surfactant headgroup is known, the radius and the concentration of the droplets are known at any composition. Assuming hard sphere interaction, the scattered intensity is calculated **_ab_** _initio_ for any composition. It turns out that the predicted scattering is very close to the observed one for the ternary system most studied so far (Aor-water-oil), but this could be a very peculiar property of the AOT molecule, whose surfactant parameter _a&_ **_U_** can vary without much energy cost. **A** linear relation (Oakenful 1980) between water content and observed radius is then obtained (Cabos and Delord 1979, 1980, Kotlarchyk **_er_** _al_ 1982). **qmax=2n/D*-rp(1-cp).** 

We have proposed recently an alternative model **(DOC** model), which is a low-resolution picture of any possible type of dispersion of water in oil or oil in water (Zemb _et al_ 1987). The DOC model is a low-resolution general model of the possible structure of micelles and microemulsions. The basic assumption of this model is that a surfactant system can be described as two ‘phases’ (oil and water) separated by an interface of constant non-zero curvature. The structure is macroscopically disordered and has local constraints given by the available volume fraction and specific area (Ninham _et a1_ 1987). 

Since microemulsion scattering does not show sharp Bragg peaks, we start with a set of Poisson points, with a distance of closest approach Dmin between them. These points are the centres of a virtual set of hard spheres of diameter Dmin. This set of Poisson points defines a complete tesselation of space in cells belonging to a random lattice (figure27). Once these random cells are constructed, _each_ cell is filled with water _and_ oil separated by a surfactant film, according to the macroscopic volume fractions. If oil is medium 1, the water (medium 2) can be distributed via three possible distributions (figure 28): 

(i) Water is located between planar bilayers along the faces of the Voronoi polyhedra in the DOC lamellar model, which looks like a foam. The prediction for this structure is that the scattering peak should move very slowly with water volume fraction, as observed with the tetradecane-DDAB-water system. Covering all the faces of the Voronoi cells induces a structure which is made of an infinity of disconnected cells, If only some of the possible faces are covered, the resulting structure is bicontinous (Cates _et a1_ 1988) and a ‘sponge’-like structure results (Warr et _a1_ 1988a). **Figure 28.** Four examples of DOC structures built from the same Voronoi lattice: **_( a )_** connectivity _2_ = 0 reduces to a set of hard spheres. _( b )_ DOC cylinder with connectivity _2_ = 2: each centre is bound to the two nearest neighbours on average. (ii) Water is distributed in spheres around the Poisson points. This is very close to hard spheres, except that some coalescence is allowed when two spheres are in contact. The connectivity of this model is _Z_ = 0. Scattering peak positions for this model can be derived (Barnes _et a1_ 1988a, b). 

(iii) Water is distributed in cylinders joining two adjacent Poisson points. Since each polyhedron has 13.4 nearest neighbours on average, a maximum number of 13 cylinders can leave a point. The average number of cylinders leaving one spherical droplet is called connectivity _Z._ Usually observed values of the connectivity are between 1 and 4. This assembly of connected cylinders and spheres is a first-order approximation of the more general random interface of constant curvature. This structure occurs whenever the spontaneous curvature is smaller than the periodicity _D*._ 

The generality of these low-resolution structural models of microemulsions is that each of these structures can be readily distinguished from the other ones by scattering experiments alone when the average chord is evaluated together with peak position as the volume fraction is varied. The DOC lamellar, cylinder and spherical models are also a quantitative generalisation of the intuitive notion of droplets coalescing into a bicontinous structure. The occurrence of three basic local geometries has been predicted for different values of the interfacial film rigidity and spontaneous curvature (Safran et _a1_ 1984). Similar thermodynamic arguments lead to the same conclusions (Porte _et al_ 1986): any structure without long-range order can be approximated locally as cylindrical, spherical or lamellar. Subtle surface chemistry effects would have to be precisely known to predict a whole phase diagram: change of counter-ion from bromide to chloride changes completely the phase diagram and the occurring structures (Gomati et _a1_ 1987).

#### _5.2. Solubilisation_ 

Solubilisation of a compound in any organised assembly (micelles, vesicles, etc) is measured by the solubilising power, which is the maximum additive-to-surfactant mole ratio in the aggregate. Exact measurement of the solubilising power is difficult, since the amount of surfactant and solute present in bulk should be taken into account, so that, for qualitative approaches, the macroscopic overall mole ratio is used instead. 

_5.2.1. Surfactant-brine-short-chain alcohol rernary systems._ These systems are precursors of microemulsions. A general coherent frame of the transition of micelles to microemulsions (structural and dynamic changes induced by alcohol) has been given by Hoffmann _et a1_ (1986). 

The most important question is the effect of short-chain alcohols on micellar structure: alcohols are used as cosurfactants to increase the solubility of oils; microemulsions with equal amounts of water and oil can only be stable if an alcohol is present. Only a few surfactants with a shape parameter _a&/u_ close to 1 are able to form stable three-component microemulsions. It is therefore crucial to understand the role of alcohols in ternary systems: is the high oil solubility mainly due to the release of steric constraints due to film flexibility or is it due to a modification of the effective _a,Z,/u_ which allows very low curvature of the interface (Ben-Shad _et al_ 1986)? 

The measurement of the partitioning of alcohol between water and micellar aggregates is the first step in any structural study, since the result allows determination of volume fractions (Stilbs 1982a, 1983, Abuin and Lissi 1983, Quirion 2nd Magid 1986, Treiner and Mannebach 1987). The determination of the concentration of the monomeric surfactant in equilibrium with the micellar aggregate is also a problem. It is known that addition of alcohol decreases the CMC (Zana **_et_** _a1_ 1981, Abu-Hamdiyyah and Rahman 1987), this would mean from a pseudo-phase model that the monomeric surfactant concentration is lowered. However, in ternary systems, the addition of alcohol increases the solubility of the surfactant in water, thus increasing the concentration of monomers (Stilbs 1982b, Hayter _et a1_ 1984, Lang and Zana 1986, De Lisi _et_ **_al_** 1987). If butanol is used as a cosurfactant, the micellar structure can be fully destroyed, the solution being a molecular dispersion (Eriksson and Lindblom 1980). 

As has been shown by contrast variation neutron scattering experiments (Hayter _et_ aZl984) in the case of pentanol solubilisation in octanoate micelles, alcohol molecules are simply adsorbed onto the micellar interface at low alcohol-to-surfactant ratio, without inducing mass modification (figure 30). As the surface gets saturated, excess pentanol penetrates into the micellar core, allowing growth of the micellar aggregate. The size distribution has been calculated from free energy evaluations and this type of mass variation is indeed expected (Ben-Shad _et a1_ 1986). The same behaviour is already known for benzene (Eriksson and Gillberg 1966, Candau and Zana 1981). **A** direct force measurement between surfactant layers with added pentanol suggests also a two-step mechanism: at low concentration, pentanol adsorbs at the interface, while it enters the surfactant layer at higher concentration (Pashley _et a1_ 1986). This ‘two-sites’ model of alcohol solubilisation provides an explanation for the solubilisation data of heptanol, in **SDS** (Russell **_ef_** _at_ 1986, Blokhus _et a1_ 1986). Adsorption and

Only one indirect Raman spectroscopic study seems to disagree with this picture of interfacial adsorption followed by penetration into the micellar core (Shih and Williams 1986). This general concept has been extended and seems also to be valid in mesophases (Boden **_et_** _al_ 1987b). At low alcohol-to-surfactant ratio, the order parameter of the hydrocarbon chains is not modified when octanol is added to the micelle (Jansson and Stilbs 1987). 

It has been noticed that the scattering of the micelles is incompatible with a model of spherical droplets at high pentanol content (Zana **_et a2_** 1983, Marignan **et** _al_ 1986). **A** locally lamellar structure is predicted by the **DOC** lamellar (foam-like) structural model in the **octylbenzenesulphonate/water/pentanol** L2 phase (Marignan **_et a1_** 1983) as the peak position in scattering experiments does not vary with water content. 

Few precise results are available about the counter-ion condensation and therefore the effective surface charge variation induced by alcohol adsorption on the interface; since the conductivity increases sharply when alcohol is added to a micelle, the surface charge is supposed to increase, due to the desorption of counter-ions. This very crude picture has recently been questioned by Hartland **_er_** _a1_ (1987). 

On the other hand, addition of alcohol has a very strong influence on micellar dynamics, as can be seen by the exchange rate of pyrene probes between micelles 

**_The structure of micelles and microemulsions_** 

329 

(Malliaris **_et_** _a1_ 1987). Three different relaxation times in chemical relaxation experiments have been observed in such a ternary system (a supplementary exchange process is observed as compared with binary systems). The exchange of pentanol is only diffusion controlled. Surfactant exchange between neighbouring micelles is greatly enhanced when cosurfactant is present. The micellar structures become very labile (Yiv **_et_** _al_ 1981) and the shape can be modified: micellar anisotropy is induced by pentanol adsorption (Hirsch **_et_** _a1_ 1984a). 

One of the most striking features in ternary systems with alcohol is the existence of an oil continuous phase, connected to the oil corner in the phase diagram, with 90% water content (Ekwall 1969, Ekwall **_et_** _al_ 1986). The structure and origin of this phase remains one of the key problems in microemulsion structure. It is expected that this phase presents locally planar interfaces from the value of the packing parameter. In our opinion these **L2** reverse micelles with very high water content should have the foam-like structure predicted by the DOC or the random surface models (see $6.1), but this remains to be proven. Lamellar phases occur generally near the water corner in phase diagrams (‘swelled’ lamellar phases) (Benton and Miller 1983, Kachar **_et a1_** 1984b, Bassereau **_et a1_** 1987). In a different system, a strongly streaming birefringent phase has been observed nearby the usual direct micellar phase L1. **A** foam-like structure identical to the DOC lamellar model has been proposed on the basis of **_q-2_** dependence of the scattering of this phase. But this is not a firm confirmation of the structure, the flat behaviour of the scattering obtained at distances up to about 500 Bragg spacings is still unexplained: alternatives exist in terms of local lamellar or cylindrical geometries, which are both shown to be allowed in thermodynamical models (Porte **_et_** _a1_ 1986). 

Although the detailed structure is not known in detail, it has been shown very recently that a statistical thermodynamic treatment can account for the occurrence of direct and reversed micelles in a ternary system. This success in reproducing a complete phase diagram together with ordered structures (lamellar and hexagonal mesophases) has been obtained by combining packing restrictions, electrostatics of counter-ions, an interfacial free energy? entropy of mixing and a hydration force at low water contents (Jonsson and Wennerstrom 1987). 

By mixing some soap and its corresponding acid other types of mixed micelles are obtained which are direct ones in water or reversed micelles in oil. The case of the sodium octanoate/octanoic acid/water system has been studied in detail (Ekwall **_et a1_** 1986). This type of mixed micelle is interesting because a mixture of salt and acid produces an aggregate of variable structural charge per unit area, since the soap has its own structural charge while the acid has none. This type of system is reminiscent of alcohol-containing ones, the alcohol being replaced by an acid. There is, however, a major difference: the surface charge density has to be constant in the systems with an acid as a cosurfactant because proton exchange between soap and acid molecules is much faster than structure reorganisation rates, any component segregation inside an aggregate is prohibited. The effective surface charge density, i.e. the charge of the surfactant headgroups less that of the counter-ion present in the hard sphere volume, was found to be independent of the chemical composition in such a system because of counter-ion condensation (Chevalier **_et_** _al_ 1985), it adjusts itself to about 8 **_pC_** cm-*. 

**_5.2.2. Other solutes in direct micelles._** Solubilisation of hydrocarbons by micellar solutions is of crucial industrial importance; not only the maximum amount of solubilised oil, but also the dynamic ratio of oil uptake are the key parameters for 

330 **_Y_** _Chevalier_ **_and_** _T Zemb_ 

efficient detergency. Due to the practical importance of this field, a large number of review papers are available (McBain and Hutchinson 1955, Ekwall _et_ **_al_** 1969a, Mukerjee 1980, Nagarajan 1986, Bayer _et_ a1 1986, Hoffmann and Ulbricht 1987). 

The picture emerging from studies on micellar solubilisation is the concept of ‘two-site localisation’: added molecules are either dissolved in the hydrocarbon core or adsorbed at the interface. This explains why polar molecules such as esters or ketones are much more soluble than hydrocarbons, as solubilising in the interfacial region (Mitra _et_ **_a1_** 1984). The ‘adsorbed’ and the ‘dissolved’ state of the host molecules have very different effects on the shape parameter _aolc/u._ The effect on the packing parameter is so strong that transition to and from liquid crystals can be induced (Sagitani and Friberg 1983). Values of adsorbed-to-dissolved mole ratio have been given by Mukerjee (1971). 

In the case of in core solubilisation, the hydrophobic volume is increased, whereas in the adsorbed state the main effect of the solute is to modify the area per surfactant headgroup _a,,_ which can be either increased by the polar part of the solute or decreased by screening the ionic headgroup repulsion. This picture explains the variation of aggregation numbers with the presence of solubilisates and the sphere-to-rod transition induced by the host molecule (Mukerjee 1980, Hoiland _et_ **_a1_** 1985). Once the sphere-torod transition has occurred, the solubilising power increases by a factor of two (Ozeki and Ikeda 1985, Imae **_et_** _a1_ 1986). Geometrical considerations also allow interpretation of the solubilisation of lipids by micelles (Lichtenberg 1985, Dennis 1986). 

The concept of two-site solubilisation should allow qualitative prediction of the solubilisation,power, expressed in numbers of host molecules per surfactant. Qualitative trends are known, but there is now a lack of any quantitative predictive theory: a much better knowledge of molecular forces is needed in order to explain simple observations. For instance, the solubility of hydrocarbons in the core of direct micelles is much lower than in the same volume of pure hydrocarbon: the physical origin of this basic observation is not known, the ‘Laplace pressure effect’ being a phenomenological explanation only. This point has been discussed by Funasaki _et a1_ (1984) for non-ionic micelles. Nevertheless, some tentative quantitative theory of solubilising power for one given micelle (SDS) (Biedermann and Datyner 1981) and a purely phenomenological but useful method of prediction of the solubility (Smith _et a1_ 1987) have been proposed. 

##### _5.3. Ternary reverse micelles using AOT_ 

_5.3.1._ **_Pure_** _reverse micelles_ of _,407, water and oil._ By far the most widely used molecule in ternary water-in-oil microemulsions (‘reverse micelle’, Lz) is AOT (sodium 1,4-bis(2-ethylhexyl) sulphosuccinate)/water/oil system. The branched geometry of the tail allows a very important water uptake in oil. In other words, the hydrophilelipophile balance is well adjusted or the shape parameter _a,lc/v_ can be close to 1 (Oakenfull 1980). **A** monograph dedicated to structure and reactivity in AOT micelles has been edited by Luisi and Straub (1984). For instance, a slight modification in the polar head structure is enough to reduce the maximum solubilised water from _w_ = 60 to less than _w_ = 6 (Faure _et_ al4985). AOT is unfortunately hydrolysed by solubilised water in a few days (Delord and Larch6 1984), producing its own short-chain cosurfactant. This is the reason why detailed phase diagrams including liquid crystalline phases are not available for **AOT.** Only approximate phase diagrams, i.e. determination of

This behaviour seems, however, very unlikely, since it would mean identical values of the chemical potential **_p N_** for very different aggregation and hydration conditions. In this latter case, it seems that the energy cost for dehydrating some **AOT** molecules 'in excess' would be large. The structure of the concentrated **L2** phase has been claimed to remain tight stacking of spherical droplets: the **AOT** microemulsion does not turn into open connected structures till the **AOT** concentration has reached 30% (Kotlarchyk **_et_** _a1_ 1984a, b, Huang and Kotlarchyk 1986). The reason for the high electrical conductivity observed above **20%** water content is therefore a balance between droplet coalescence and core exchanges. **A** detailed study of the electrical percolation threshold and the relation with droplet concentration fluctuations near the critical point has shown that a dynamical percolation between spherical droplets occurs (Grest **_et_** _al_ 1985, Peyrelasse **_et_** _a1_ 1988). 

Reviews about structural results in **AOT** reverse micelles are available (Eicke and Kvita 1984, Chen and Kotlarchyk 1985). 

**A** rough comparison of the scattering of hard spheres shows that some attractive potential between the droplets has to be considered (Safran and Turkevich 1983, Kotlarchyk **_et_** _a1_ 1984a, Robinson **_et_** _a1_ 1984, Toprakcioglu **_et_** _a1_ 1984). In the case of **AOT,** the existence of a critical point has been demonstrated (Huang and Kim 1981) in non-penetrating solvents such as decane, but has not been observed in octane (Kotlarchyk **_et_** _a1_ 1983). 

However, the physical origin of the attractive intermicellar potential, probably related to hydrophobic chain interpenetration, remains unclear: for instance, no theory accounts for the differences in critical compositions and temperatures for different oils. The only general rule is that the attractive interaction is proportional to the interpenetration of the two surfactant layers when reverse micelles come into contact (Lemaire **_et_** _al_ 1983): this very simple interaction potential gives the right variation in water/oil reverse micelles for different penetrating oils. By taking into account the interpenetration of the chains and van der Waals interactions between the water droplets, the virial 

_The structure of micelles and microemulsions_ 

333 

coefficients could be fitted for different water droplet radii (and also added alcohol supposed to reduce chain interdigitation in quaternary microemulsions) (Brunetti _et_ **_al_** 1983, Roux _et al_ 1984a, b). Another interpretation attributes the observed attraction to solvent-induced interactions (Pincus and Safran 1987). 

Some authors refuse to admit the necessity of this attractive interaction potential to explain the presence of critical points in the phase diagrams, explaining the high scattering at low **_q_** by a high polydispersity of the droplet size (Kotlarchyk _et a1_ 1988). An interpretation of the scattering due to a polydisperse set of hard spheres could even be reconciled with thermodynamical arguments developed by Safran (1983) and Stecker and Benedek (1984). Indeed, the origin of the attractive potential is not well understood since the measurement by any scattering technique cannot separate polydipersity from attractive interaction effects. However, the attractive interactions are important, since polydispersity cannot induce liquid-gas equilibria in the phase diagram. In the absence of explanation of the origin of these attractive interactions, Huang _et_ **_al_** (1984) could explain the whole scattering curve by using a square well attractive potential of **1.5kT** with a range of 1.1 times the micellar radius. 

These attractive interactions induce the formation of micelle clusters; when micelles coalesce a continuous water path can be formed which explains the electrical percolation threshold observed with increasing water content (Eicke _et a1_ 1986). 

The measurement of the counter-ion distribution inside the micelles' water core has been attempted, but no clear conclusion could be drawn because of the low resolution of small-angle x-ray scattering (Cabos and Marignan 1985). 

Reactivity studies in the core of reverse micelles show two very different behaviours according to the water-to-surfactant ratio **_w:_** below 10 water molecules per **AOT** molecule, water is bound to surfactant headgroups and counter-ions. When _w_ exceeds 10, 'bulk' water appears and reactivity constants (such as hydrated electron life time) characteristic of bulk water are observed (Pileni _et a1_ 1982). The state of the water molecules has been investigated by NMR: six water molecules per dissociated counterion and three per ionic headgroup are immobilised (Wong and Thomas 1977, Wong _et al_ 1977), a correct evaluation of water dynamics requires, however, a more complete model than simple isotropic rotation and multiple-frequency experiments carried out with different observable nuclei ('H, **'H,** _"0)_ (Llor and Rigny 1986). Rotational isomerism on the headgroups allows a slight variation of the interfacial area per surfactant headgroup. Isomeric rotation is dependent on the water content and the nature (penetrating or non-penetrating) of the oil (Maitra and Eicke 1981, Martin and Magid 198 1). This observation is very important and may be the key to understanding the unique ability of AOT to dissolve water in oil: the molecular conformation adjusts for providing an _aolc/v_ value imposed by external conditions, the origin of **AOT'S** solubilising properties being due to its flexibility at a molecular level. 

Recently, a molecular dynamics simulation of an aggregate of 72 model surfactant molecules and 1072 molecules of water has been shown to have the following properties: the water pool is a spherical cavity on average with significant roughening of the interface (Brown and Clarke 1988). The outermost water molecules are not hydrogen bonded but strongly coordinated to the counter-ion adsorbed at the interface. The significant solvent penetration into the interface is probably an artefact due to the modelling of the whole surfactant tail as a single spherical bead. 

_5.3.2. Solubilisation_ **_of_** _additices in reverse micelles._ Addition of solutes to reverse micelles results in quaternary systems, but the results are given here, because the basic structure of the water droplets remains after small additions of solute. **A** solute can 

**334** **_Y Chevalier and T_** _Zemb_ 

be located in the water core, in the interfacial region or in the bulk solvent. Solute distribution within these three locations has been indirectly obtained by means of fluorescence experiments (Encinas and Lissi 1986). 

However, at low additive concentration, the basic structure of spheres interacting through a hard sphere and a slight attractive potential holds and one is interested in the perturbation of the structure by the additive. Since the radius of the water droplet is fixed by the polar volume and the available interface, four different types of solubilisation can induce four different types of structure perturbation (Pileni **_et_** _a1_ 1985a). From simple geometrical arguments, it is possible to deduce the solute location from the perturbation (figure 33).

335 

(i) **If** solubilisation occurs in the polar volume, its effect is mainly an increase of the average size of the micelle. This case has been observed with chymotrypsin: (ii) If the solute is located at the interface, adsorption is equivalent to addition of surfactant, thus decreasing the micellar radius. This has been observed with cytochrome c. 

(iii) If the solute dissolves in the solvent, no structure modification is expected: this has been observed with diethylether. 

(iv) If the micelle is too small to receive a solute molecule without deformation, i.e. at low water content, a segregation occurs between small empty micelles and large objects which are mainly hydrated proteins covered with surfactant (Zampieri _et a1_ 1986, Chatenay _et_ **_a1_** 1987). 

Chatenay has also shown that intermicellar interactions are strongly modified by the presence of a solute. Sheu _et_ **_a1_** (1986) confirmed that at high water content **_(w_** > 20) a model with two populations of micelles is not needed for data interpretation and that solubilisation of cytochrome in reverse micelles induces an increase of droplet average radius. 

The attractive interaction potential between reverse micelles is also strongly modified by the presence of the solute. The presence of alcohols as additives in the interfacial layer modifies the demixing temperature (‘cloud point’) and the low-q region of the scattering (Howe _et_ **_al_** 1986). **As** the ‘cloud point’ is reached by heating, a demixing into a dilute and a concentrated **L2** phase occurs. **As** micelles have an identical size in both coexisting phases, the behaviour is similar to a liquid-gas equilibrium. When initial concentration and temperature are set so that the upper and lower concentrations are equal, a critical point is reached. In that context, the physics of reverse micelles is similar to that of pure molecular fluids. 

Reverse micelles are very useful systems in biotechnology: it has been shown that whole bacteria _(E. coli)_ can be solubilised and remain active in reverse micelles (Haering _et_ **_al_** 1985). Reverse micelles as a bioseparation tool have been reviewed by Kadam (1986). **A** general review about hosts in reverse micelles has recently been published (Luisi _et a1_ 1988). 

##### **_5.4._** _Mixed micelles_ 

When two different surfactants are used together, the resulting structure is called a mixed micelle. 

Mixtures of surfactants behave very differently from what would be predicted from the properties of their pure components: mixtures are not ideal. This can be simply shown by the measurement of the CMC of a mixture of two surfactants: the CMC of a mixture does not vary linearly with the composition (Bourrel _ef_ **_a1_** 1984, Hoiland _et_ **_a1_** 1985). Theories giving the composition of aggregates from the CMC variation with overall chemical composition of the mixture are available (Rubingh 1979, Hua and Rosen 1982, Nagarajan 1985, Nguyen _et a1_ 1986). 

Indeed, the properties of a mixed micelle system depend mainly on the interaction of polar headgroups, which can be detected by volumetric studies (Funasaki _et a1_ 1986). Mixtures of surfactants with identical headgroups and different chain lengths are close to ideality. Strong deviations are observed with mixtures of ionic and non-ionic surfactants or cationic-anionic mixtures. Mixing cationic and anionic surfactants often results in an insoluble precipitate, but this is not always the case (Hoffmann and 

336 **_Y Chevalier_** _and T_ **_Zemb_** 

Ulbricht 1987). The structure of these micelles differs from classical micelles. Interacting rodlike micelles are formed at low concentration. When salt is added, the stiff rods turn progressively into flexible ones, giving a viscoelastic character to the solution (Hoffmann **_er_** _a1_ 1983). These rodlike micelles are charged since the micelle chemical composition is not a 1-1 mixture. The presence of connected rods has been deduced from the observation of a scattering peak at very small angles. This system follows the prediction of the DOC model for a connectivity **_2_** = 2. The size of the flexible rods first increases, and then decreases with concentration because of the very strong intermicellar repulsions (Hoffmann and Ulbricht 1987). This situation is analogous to the vesicle-to-micelle transition, which was surprisingly observed with increasing concentration (Ninham **_er_** _a1_ 1983b, Brady **_er_** _a1_ 1984). At higher concentration, above a transition composition detected as a break in the conductivity, the structure turns to uncharged dislike micelles being 1- 1 anionic-cationic surfactant mixtures in the aggregates. 

The field of mixed micelles made of non-ionic and ionic surfactants together is still an open field in terms of structural studies, even if these types of mixture are very widely used in industrial applications. A simple picture of interacting spherical droplets cannot account for light scattering experiments (GuCring **_er_** _a1_ 1985). Theoretical expressions of the counter-ion binding to such mixed aggregates has been proposed by Rathman and Scamehorn (1987). The concentration of monomers in equilibrium with mixed micelles and interaction parameters between molecules can be evaluated from CMC values of mixed systems (Asakawa **_er_** _a1_ 1985, Hey **_er a1_** 1985, Wall and Elvingston 1985). 

##### **_5.5. Double-chain cationic surfactants_** 

Double-chain cationic surfactants are convenient for studying three-component microemulsions (without cosurfactant). The prototype of this type of surfactant is didodecyldimethylammonium bromide **(DDAB),** more than 50% of oil can solubilise in water with **DDAB,** the same amount as with AOT (Angel **_et_** _a1_ 1983). The phase diagrams show a very large **L2** domain, which is very stable since **DDAB** is not beset with hydrolysis problems (Fontell **_et a1_** 1986). **DDAB** is nearly insoluble in water and oil, ternary mixtures with **DDAB** are therefore an ideal microemulsion model system (figure **34).** 

The phase diagrams have been explored, together with the ordered anisotropic phases appearing around the large microemulsion phase (Fontell **_er_** _a1_ 1986). The differences between phase diagrams obtained in ternary systems with different oils are explained by the different oil uptake by the hydrocarbon tails (Ninham **_et a1_** 1984, Evans **_et_** _a1_ 1986b). A large number of structures can be built up with these types of surfactant since the packing parameter is close to one. Phase diagrams have been studied by shortening one or two of the surfactant tails. For the system didecyldimethylammonium bromide/water/hexane, a new type of demixing between two **L2** phases has been demonstrated: two microemulsions are in equibrium, far from any critical point since temperature has no effect on that demixing (Warr **_er_** _a1_ 1988b). 

The electrical conductivity shows inverse percolation behaviour at low water content: as water is added, the conductivity decreases by orders of magnitude at a volume fraction which depends on the type of oil (Chen **_et al_** 1984, Blum **_et al_** 1985). **A** structure as thin cylinders has therefore been proposed (Chen **er** **_a1_** 1986). It is the only one compatible with the interfacial tension behaviour, due to strong correlations between parallel conducting thin cylinders of oil (Allen **_et_** _a1_ 1987). These disordered

open connected cylinders have been the first example of a DOC cylinder model: the structure can be described as a network of connected cylinders laid on a virtual Voronoi lattice (Zemb _et a1_ 1987). This network of connected cylinders, of connectivity close to 2 (figure **35),** is the first model compatible with the x-ray scattering peak position (Ninham _et a1_ 1987). Once the constraint of maximal local curvature is added, the percolation threshold and the limit of the L2 phase can be explained by purely geometrical arguments (Barnes _et a1_ 1987b). 

Another consequence of the high sensitivity of this packing parameter close to one (i.e. spontaneous curvature near to zero) is that any slight change in counter-ions has enormous effects on the phase diagrams (Chen _et al_ 1987). The most striking case is the substitution of the bromide counter-ion by hydroxide, which makes the surfactant soluble in water. At low water content, didodecyldimethylammonium hydroxide spontaneously forms unilamellar vesicles in water (Ninham _et a1_ 1983b, Brady _et a1_ 1984, Kachar **_et_** _a1_ 1984a). At high water content, these vesicles shrink because of the high electrostatic interactions, turning back to micelles. It was commonly accepted that in dilute binary solutions, monomers are in equilibrium with spherical micelles; the picture that emerges slowly from studies on ternary microemulsions is that unilamellar vesicles can be in equilibrium with micelles. The origin of this behaviour in terms of free energy remains to be elucidated. 

##### _5.6. Non-ionic surfactant/oil/water ternary systems_ 

Non-ionic surfactant polar headgroups are generally made of polyoxyethylene: these groups are hydrated with one to two water molecules per oxyethylene group. Steric constraints are less drastic than for ionic surfactants: area per polar head and chain length are able to adapt for different compositions. Therefore, the possibility of a large

stability domain of single-phase microemulsion exists. At low temperature, the nonionic surfactant is soluble in water whereas at higher temperature the surfactant is soluble in oil: a certain temperature range around the phase inversion temperature allows then for three phase equilibria with middle phases without addition of cosurfactant. The phase diagrams of these systems are known (Kahlweit **_et_** _al_ 1983, 1985). 

General trends of the interfacial area per non-ionic headgroup versus volume fraction, which is the crucial measurement for structure investigation, are not yet known. A lower consolute point exists in binary solutions, where a simple model of interacting droplets holds to explain scattering spectra up to a concentration of 25% of surfactant. 

##### **_5.7._** _Polymer-micelle mixtures_ 

Most studies deal with water-soluble polymers in direct micelles. This is not micellar solubilisation but polymer adsorption at the micellar surface. 

When the polymer solution **(PEO)** is dilute, the polymer is adsorbed around the SDS micelles. These keep the spontaneous size occurring in pure water (Cabane 1977). Opposite conclusions, i.e. smaller micelles, have been inferred since then for the same system by indirect methods (Gilyani and Wolfram 1981) and fluorescence probe studies (Zana _et al_ 1985). 

When the polymer is semidilute, two different structures in the polymer/micelle solution have been identified for the polyoxyethylene-sDs system (Cabane and Duplessix 1987): at high polymer-to-micelle ratio, the micellar structure is not perturbed 

**_The_** _structure_ **_of_** _micelles and microemulsions_ 

339 

by the polymer. The presence of the polymer network does not perturb the set **of** interacting globular micelles. 

At lower polymer-to-micelle ratio, one has necklaces of polymers decorated by SDS micelles: one observes a very peculiar scattering curve with two correlation peaks moving with different scaling laws towards concentration (Cabane and Duplessix 1985, 1987). The polymer strands are therefore seen as the origin of an attractive interaction between micelles: the system is a semidilute solution of independent necklaces (figure **_36)._** 

The complex formed between bovine serum albumin and lithium dodecylsulphate micelles has been studied by Chen and Teixeira (1986). At high surfactant concentration the protein is denaturated, as are most proteins with ionic surfactants. From the linear behaviour of the logarithm of the intensity, a ‘fractal’ structure has been attributed to the protein-micelle aggregate. This is not the case when non-denaturating non-ionic surfactants are used: in the rhodopsin-detergent complex, the apolar part of the rhodopsin is in the core of the large non-ionic micelles (Osborne **er** **_a1_** 1978). 

Mixtures of polyelectrolytes and micelles have just started to be studied by an exploration of the phase diagram (Dubin _et a1_ 1985, Dubin and Davis 1985). Polyionmixed micelle complexes have been detected. The main parameter controlling the phase diagram is the surface charge density of the micelles, which can be set by the anionic-to-non-ionic ratio in the surfactant mixture used. ##### **_6._ Quaternary** systems 

Isotropic solutions made of four chemical components are very complicated systems: the complete phase diagram needs to be represented in a tetrahedron and is often not available. Most systems are composed of a surfactant, a cosurfactant and two solvents: water and some kind of oil. The cosurfactant is usually a single-chain alcohol, although the interesting case of amine has been studied by Wormuth and Kaler (1987). 

##### _6.1. Current models_ of _microemulsion microstructure_ 

The terms ‘bicontinuous’, ‘bicontiguous’ or ‘random’ structure are used in most papers, but there is a lack of quantitative structural geometrical relations allowing a clear distinction between these intuitive concepts. Here, we give the main aspects of the most widely used structural models for which predictions can be tested experimentally (figure **37):** 

(i) The first intuition of a bicontinuous structure is due to Scriven (1976, 1977). Since the diffusion coefficients of water and oil are both high (Kaler _et al_ 1983a, b, Clarkson _et a1_ 1985, GuCring and Liildman 1985, Lindman and Stilbs 1987), some continuity must exist between the water and oil domains. Since birefringence or Bragg

(c) Scriven **(1977):** two examples of bicontinuous mesophase-like structures with minimal interfacial area. 

**_The structure of micelles and microemulsions_** 

341 

peaks are not observed, the structure cannot be macroscopically ordered. Therefore, the microemulsion must be some kind of molten cubic phase. There was no experimental evidence of that idea at that time, nor was the model quantitative. 

(ii) The first quantitative model of microemulsion is the Talmon and Prager model (Talmon and Prager 1978, 1982, Kaler and Prager 1982). The rules for constructing such a bicontinuous model are the following: first choose a set of random points (Poisson points); these points define a complete tesselation of space in adjacent cells (Voronoi tesselation). Each point in space belongs to the cell centred at the closest Poisson point. This is a very general method of generating a ‘random lattice’ whose geometrical properties have been studied extensively (Meijering 1953). Then, fill at random the cells with water or oil, according to the global volume fractions of water and oil. The surfactant film volume fraction is considered as negligible and surfactant film is distributed only along the faces common to two adjacent cells filled with different phases. 

The great success of the Talmon-Prager model has been to generate an average size of the resulting oil and water domains which are of the order of magnitude of the observed size (Talmon and Prager 1982). It was the first available quantitative model which could be tested, since a clever method for deriving an analytical form of the scattering was worked out by Kaler and Prager (1982). But there are two major drawbacks: the conductivity of microemulsions should always exhibit percolation behaviour instead of the non-monotonic one observed in some systems and no peak should occur in the observed scattering. Unfortunately, except for few samples very close to a critical point, there is always a peak in the observed scattering. The Talmon-Prager model cannot represent the structure of a microemulsion as noticed by many authors (Zemb **_et_** _a1_ 1987, Vonk **_et_** _al_ 1988, Teubner and Strey 1987). 

The Talmon and Prager model has been improved by de Gennes and Taupin (1982) in the case where the spontaneous curvature is nearly zero: in that case, the characteristic length & is large (about 50 nm) and close to the size set by the low surfactant content. In that case, an approximate model of structure is the following: the random polyhedra are replaced (for the sake of simplicity in order to evaluate the phase diagram) by cubic cells, filled at random with water and oil, according to the macroscopic volume fraction set by composition. This is called the CRC (cubic random cell) model. The spontaneous average curvature & is then given by the film bending energy 

where **_KO_** is the film elasticity constant and **_a_** is a molecular size (the lower cut-off wavelength of the film undulations). The microemulsion is stable when the spontaneous length & is of the same order of magnitude as the size set by the volume fraction **_cp_** and the available area **C** (see below). 

This curvature allows a natural scaling **of** the system, whose structure is approximated as follows: construct a regular lattice of cubes, of edge length &, filled at random with a probability given by the macroscopically imposed volumes of water and oil. **As** in the Talmon-Prager model, the interface is located at the edges of the cubic elementary cells (de Gennes and Taupin 1982). This model has essentially been built in order to allow calculation of phase diagrams, and this was made by Widom (1984a, b), who showed that the Winsor I-Winsor 11-Winsor 111 behaviour can be obtained with CRC structure; it was further refined by Safran **_et a1_** (1986).

Strictly speaking, the **CRC** model does not predict a peak in the observed scattering because a zero in the scattering of the individual cube wipes out the Bragg peak given by the cubic lattice. If any thermal disorder in the underlying perfect cubic lattice is introduced, however, a peak appears at the position related to the cube edge length **_a,_** given by 

_q_ = 27r/a. 

The **CRC** model has been compared with the observed scattering by Auvray **_et al_** (1984a, b). Qualitatively, the behaviour is correct; a peak appears in the scattering and the variation of the peak position is approximately predicted by the **CRC** model. _Also,_ bicontinuous structures can be stable (Schick and Wei-Heng 1986) and one can observe three phase equilibria (Widom 1984a, b). Both the **CRC** and Talmon-Prager models are compatible with the high self-diffusion coefficients of oil and water in the same sample in concentrated microemulsions (Lindman **_et_** a1 1981, GuCring and Lindman 1985). Results of quasi-elastic light scattering too can be understood with these models (Chang and Kaler 1986), but the scattering peak position with the **CRC** model is systematically wrong by a factor of 1.5 to 3. Moreover, with the **CRC** model as with the Talmon-Prager model, the conductivity should always vary monotonically with composition. As shown by Auvra.y, a basic feature of the **CRC** model has to be modified to agree with the observed scattering: the cube edge length, instead of being fixed by the spontaneous curvature, should rather be set, as in ternary systems, by the available interface; the cube edge length is therefore dependent on the specific area covered by surfactant instead of the spontaneous curvature, and is given by

The non-monotonic behaviour of the conductivity, already noticed by Baker **_et al_** (1984), is incompatible with the **CRC** or Talmon-Prager models, as is the observation of a long-range distance obtained in the Patterson function of the scattered intensity (De Geyer 1987). The conductivity shows a maximum in the middle of the **L2** phase: this is a general feature which appears in three different systems where the surfactant is **SDS,** potassium oleate or AOT (Boned **_et_** al1980,1982). In some cases, the conductivity does not show a maximum but a percolation threshold which can be related to percolation of small spherical droplets (Lagues **_et_** _a1_ 1978). 

The position of the scattering peak in Winsor 111 microemulsions is incompatible with the **CRC** model and could be explained in a rough approximation as a molten cubic phase, thus indicating a local complexity in terms of assembly of ‘distorted minimal curvature’ surfaces (De Geyer 1987). The same observation was also made earlier by Parodi (1984): here a locally lamellar structure is constructed. With these two models, the scattering curve can be reproduced assuming a very short correlation length of the local structure. 

The DOC model of microemulsions has been introduced to explain the behaviour of ternary systems (see **9** 5). This model takes into account the fact that there is more interfacial area for a given structure than expected from other structural models. In the case where the volume fraction and the butanol partition can be calculated from dilution experiments, Abillon **_er_** al (1988) have shown that the peak position and the average chords in a quaternary system are compatible with the DOC model in the case of cylinders. The effect of the alcohol partition between interfacial film, water and oil is measured by a variation of the self-diffusion coefficient (Ceglie **_et_** al1987). If butanol is used as cosurfactant, the molecular exchange is so rapid that all macroscopic

**343** 

self-diffusion coefficients are high, suggesting that butanol destroys the organisation of interfacial film (Stilbs 1983). 

In another quaternary system, Vonk **_et_** _al_ (1988) have shown that the scattering could be calculated on the absolute scale for a large set of compositions, assuming only two parameters: thickness of local lamellar structure, and an orientational order parameter between the normals to planes. The distortion length found is on the order of **50** nm, and the direction persistence length on the order of 25 nm, as predicted by the DOC lamellar model (Zemb **_et_** _al_ 1987, Barnes **_et a1_** 1988a, b). **A** similar local lamellar structure has been proposed in the sDs/butanol/toluene/brine system by Bellocq **_et a1_** (1979) and Bellocq and Fourche (1980). 

Another model of microemulsions has been proposed by Berk (1987): a striking feature of neutron scattering of microemulsions is that they give a peak when oil or water is deuterated but the peak sometimes disappears when one observes the scattering of the film alone (both deuterated water and oil). This feature could be explained by exhibiting a random structure built by random interfering waves (Cahn 1965). This study showed that a bicontinuous structure can be constructed, avoiding the phase problem, by setting the volume fraction and the observed scattering. Two-dimensional analogues of microemulsions have been constructed in order to show that one can move continuously from water-in-oil to oil-in-water droplets while keeping the scattering strictly constant: the fact that the observed **_I ( 4 )_** does not vary even when conductivity varies by orders of magnitude is demonstrated (Welberry and Zemb 1988). 

**A** mechanical model of microemulsions came to the conclusion that within the same ‘phase’ in the phase diagram, different structures can coexist and transform continuously into each other: short cylinders towards spheres and local distorted lamellae (Neogi et _al_ 1987). This model has not yet been compared with experiments due to lack of quantitative predictions. 

The quaternary systems are mostly studied in the region of the phase diagram which is poor in surfactants, keeping realistic industrial applications such as detergency or oil recovery in mind. Since the complete phase diagram is a tetrahedron, it is usual to represent a slice of it, which is called pseudo-ternary phase diagram. Some ratio has to be fixed: the traditional way is to represent a projection of the phase diagram at constant surfactant-to-cosurfactant ratio. It is known that the water-to-surfactant ratio **_w_** is a good thermodynamic variable: the ratio w of water to surfactant is the same in two coexisting phases in a multiphasic region. Limits of a single-phase region often correspond to a constant w value; therefore, a representation at constant **_w_** is preferred (Cebula **_et_** _al_ 1982). The same ratio **_w_** is a field variable in critical fluctuations (Roux and Bellocq 1984). Indeed, a given ratio w corresponds to a fixed average curvature (Friberg and Buraszenka 1978). This value is called the spontaneous radius of curvature. For ternary systems, the spontaneous curvatures H and _K_ are given by

because the sphere radius, the average mean and Gaussian curvatures are the same **_( R_** = _H_ = **_K ) ._** This radius is then equal to the persistence length &. If H is different from **_K,_** a common approximation is to assume that & = H. In ternary systems, **(k** is

Interfacial chain length 1 is not modified but the area per surfactant headgroup increases by about **0.2** nm2 per alcohol molecule penetrating into the interfacial film. 

The second important parameter to the microemulsion structure has different names in the literature. It can be intuitively understood as 'granularity' of the structure or 'cell size' or 'periodicity'. In the case where a peak is seen in the scattering at a value **_q*,_** the cell size **_D"_** is given by

But a cell size _D*_ can also be defined without any peak in the scattering: the inverse interfacial area per unit volume **1/S** is a natural length in the system. **1/S** is, however, only an order of magnitude, the exact value of the cell size is given at fixed interfacial area and volume fraction by the peak position. If the structure of the microemulsion reduces to a dispersion of spheres, & is the radius of the spheres where **_D"_** corresponds to the average distance between spheres: each sphere is at the centre of a Voronoi cell.

**A** common simplifying assumption is that the saddle-splay term depending on **_I?_** is negligible compared with the bending energy depending upon **_KO._** This is only valid in favourable cases, but up to now no general theory which assumes that the two terms are equally important is available. The value of **_KO_** can be evaluated by optical methods, assuming that the roughness of the interface between coexisting phases is related to **_KO_** (Meunier 1985). The result of these studies shows that the value of **_KO_** is much higher for ternary systems **_(KO> kT)_** than for quaternary ones where **_KO> kT_** holds. **A** similar conclusion has been drawn from electric and magnetic birefringence measurements (Meyer _et a1_ 1982). 

This allows us to introduce a reduced temperature _r_ as 

_r_ = _T/2n-Ko._ 

When the reduced temperature ~ < 1 a zero-temperature model can be used: the , spontaneous curvature is constant throughout the structure. Predicted microstructures are expected to be lamellar, cylindrical or spherical (Safran **_et al_** 1984). In that case, the DOC model developed for ternary systems applies. If & is lower than _D",_ the microstructure can be approximated to connected cylinders (DOC cylinder model) (Ninham _er a!_ 1987). If **tk** is larger than _D",_ a sponge-like structure is expected (Cates _er nl_ 1988). The intermediate case is difficult: the best model could be a disordered dispersion of Voronoi cells, filled with either water or oil (Talmon and Prager 1982, Schick and Wei-Heng 1986, Andelmann **er** **_a1_** 1987). Indeed, the flexibility of the film is very low and both distances & and _D"_ can be reduced to a single distance & and the original CRC model is used with a size-dependent bending constant.
