**345** 

If **_T >_** 1, then thermal fluctuations are important: the interface has a bending radius which is no longer constant at every point and thermal fluctuations wipe out geometrical constraints. No geometrical model of microstructure holds any more. The dispersion has to be described in terms **of** cells whose size is fixed by geometrical constraints. Some arbitrary energy terms have to be associated with local contiguity of water and oil domains (Andelmann **_et_** _a1_ 1987, Welberry and Zemb 1988, Milner **_et_** _a1_ 1988). 

The phenomenological expression derived by Teubner and Strey (1987) for ternary systems can also be used here. In ternary systems, the persistence length does not vary with concentration whereas addition of butanol allows a large variation of & with concentration. 

At high reduced temperature, if the persistence length **(k** is large and the volume fractions are low, a dispersion of lamellae, without long-range order is predicted in the region between the microemulsion and the lamellar phase (Cates **_et a1_** 1988). This phase has indeed been observed (Porte **_et a1_** 1986) and is of crucial importance: its recent discovery creates a continuous conceptual path between micelles, microemulsions and vesicles. Geometrical rules for construction of a random dispersion of lamellae are the following: 

(i) Divide space into a cubic lattice (for calculation of a phase diagram) or into a Voronoi tesselation (for structural investigations). The lattice size is set by interfacial area and volumes. 

(ii) Fill the cells with two ‘species’ of oil, species 1 and 2. These species are of course really identical. The species are distributed at random within the lattice. The only parameter is the ‘pseudo-volume fraction’ $ of species 1. 

(iii) If two adjacent cells are filled with different ‘species’ of oil, the interface between them is a thin layer of water covered by two surfactant films. The cells are filled with the major solvent. 

**In** the following, we refer to these construction rules as the random lamellar model. The resulting structure is a disordered ‘sponge’ of water in oil. If **I)** is about 0.5, the structure is close to a folded and compressed sheet of paper. The interfacial film is continuous, it has no edge. For low $, the structure turns naturally towards dilute vesicles (Cates **_et_** _ul_ 1988). 

##### **_6.2. Experimental evidence_** 

A review devoted to experimental methods of studying microemulsions is available (Kahlweit **_et_** _a1_ 1987). Some observations on the structure of microemulsions can be directly measured by scattering without use of any model. These points are direct evidence obtained with x-ray or light scattering, and are more powerful than indirect measurement obtained by spectroscopic methods. These are: 

(i) The direct measurement of the average radius of curvature by Auvray **_et_** _‘ul_ (1984a, b) in the system sDs/H,O/butanol/oil. When the oil and water have equal volume fractions, the average radius **of** curvature is zero. There is no information about the Gaussian curvature of the interface. 

(ii) The direct comparison of the average chord through the structure towards the position of the scattering peak: the **CRC** model and all models filling random cells predict these two quantities to be equal. Locally lamellar, hard sphere and **DOC** models predict the observed ratio of 2 between these two quantities. 

346 **_Y_** _Chevalier_ **_and T_** _Zemb_ 

Up to now, there is no quaternary system whose microstructure is understood well enough to derive the scattering from composition alone. The problem is that volume fraction and specific interface **_S_** cannot be precisely determined. If one uses a model of ellipsoids (as in Caponetti _et al_ (1986)), any scattering curve can be fitted to interacting monodisperse ellipsoids. The good agreement between fitted scattering curves and experiment is therefore not a definite proof of a structural model. 

Quantitative determination of the microstructure in quaternary systems is very difficult because there are four components which are distributed in three pseudophases: the water phase, which contains a negligible proportion of surfactant, the oil phase and the surfactant film, where most of the surfactant molecules are located. The main problem is the distribution of the alcohol between these three pseudo-phases (Biais _er a1_ 1981, 1986). In the pseudo-phase framework, one can always remove one of the three pseudo-phases, for instance the interfacial film. Therefore, it should always be possible to find a surfactant-free ternary solution with the same vapour pressure as the complete four-component microemulsion. This hypothesis holds as a first approximation in all systems studied so far. 

Another approach consists (for some favourable cases, i.e. near the water or the oil corner of the phase diagram) in diluting the microemulsion at constant droplet size with an appropriate mixture of oil and surfactant. A correct trajectory in the multicomponent phase diagram has thus to be defined where the diluent chemical composition is the same as that of the continuous phase. The procedure consists in a dilution along (close to) a diphasic domain boundary in such a way that the overall composition of additions remains constant (Schulman _et a1_ 1959, Graciaa _et_ **_a1_** 1976, 1977, 1978). It is supported by the observation that the water-to-surfactant ratio is constant along a demixing line in water-in-oil microemulsion phase diagrams, this ratio governing the size if the area per headgroup is constant (Roux 1984, Roux and Bellocq 1984). The particle size is expected to reach its maximum value along such a pathway, further growth causing instability and phase separation. Under such a dilution procedure, the chemical potentials of all the components remain constant. The constant chemical composition of droplets has been checked by experiments (Lagues _et al_ 1978), but interactions may influence droplet size, even at constant composition (Cazabat 1983). Another problem is that the proximity of critical points has to be avoided. This dilution procedure has allowed light scattering studies of the interaction between droplets (Cazabat 1983). At high dilution, near the water corner or near the oil corner, hard sphere interaction gives a good approximation of the scattering (Cebula **_et_** _al_ 1982). In this latter paper, interpretations concerning concentrated systems are, however, questionable, since the interparticle scattering was oversimplified. 

Some systems can be considered as pseudo-ternary systems, where brine replaces pure water in the composition of the sample. Adding salt is a very handy way of testing the importance of electrostatics in microemulsions since the two main effects of salt addition are to screen out the electrostatic interactions and to reduce the area per headgroup, thus varying the spontaneous curvature and the packing parameter _u/aoZc_ introduced to roughly predict the phase behaviour. This has been predicted in the first zero-order geometrical unified theory of micelles, microemulsions and vesicles (Mitchell and Ninham 1981), where the theory of self-aggregation is extended from micelles to vesicles and microemulsions. The main observed trends with temperature variation, oil type variation or salt concentration are explained with the effective packing parameter _v/aol,._ Predictions have been verified in terms of extension of the stability region of single-phase microemulsions: _u/aolc_ has to be increased close to 

**_The structure of micelles and microemulsions_** 

347 

unity with a flexible interface in order to allow a large single-phase microemulsion (Lang **_et a1_** 1984). This observation is called ‘chain length compatibility’ (Bansal **_et al_** 1980, Leung **_et al_** 1986). Since the **_u/aolc_** parameter of common single-chain surfactants is lower than one, addition of small quantities of quaternary ammonium surfactants increases the spontaneous radius of curvature in SDS microemulsions (Sauterey **_et_** _a1_ 1978). 

The salinity variation is an easy way of varying the geometrical packing parameter **_u/aOlc_** and hence the behaviour of a pseudo-quaternary system (since brine is used instead of pure water). At low salt content, one has equilibrium between microemulsion and excess oil (Winsor I), then a microemulsion in equilibrium with excess water and oil (Winsor 111) and finally, at salinities of the order of 50 g **I-’,** excess water in equilibrium with a microemulsion (Winsor 11). Usually, the term ‘middle phase’ refers to the microemulsion part of a Winsor **I11** system. This ‘Winsor’ behaviour occurs in most systems, but not always: two microemulsion phases in equilibrium are sometimes observed (Roux **_et_** _a1_ 1983b). If the microstructure remains as spherical droplets, this phase behaviour can be understood in terms of van der Waals attraction between droplets (Huh 1984), but the same behaviour can occur with any other microstructure. The structure of quaternary microemulsions seems to be very close to perfectly monodisperse spheres of oil in water near the oil corner (roughly more than 95% of oil) or near the water corner of the phase diagram. When the picture of closed droplets holds, the microemulsion is called water-in-oil (LJ or oil-in-water (L,) microemulsion, the minor compound is supposed to be located ‘inside’. **A** detailed review of the structure and the thermodynamics of microemulsions in these ‘dilute’ cases is available (Bellocq **_et_** _a1_ 1984). For water-in-oil **(L2)** microemulsions, the dilution procedure at the boundary of a demixing curve was used in a large number of light, x-ray and neutron scattering studies about the structure in the dilute water-in-oil regime: the emerging picture is that the spherical droplets interact through an attractive potential which is due to the chain overlapping (Cazabat and Langevin 1981, Bellocq **_et_** aZ1984, Huang **_et_** _al_ 1984, Dichristina **_et_** _al_ 1985). Evidence has been obtained for liquid gas transitions and critical points due to this attraction (Fourche **_et_** _a1_ 1982, Cazabat **_et_** _aZ_ 1982a). The relationship between critical points and percolation thresholds has been studied (Cazabat **_et_** _a1_ 1984a). The effect of critical concentration fluctuations of attractive droplets near a coexistence curve allows the calculation of the observed scattering curve over four decades in intensity for the cTAB/octane/butano~/brine system (Magid **_et_** _al_ 1984b). 

The problem of microemulsion microstructure is much more complicated in the centre of the phase diagram, where any conductivity or molecular diffusion measurement suggests a ‘bicontinuous’ structure (Lindman **_et_** _a1_ 1980a, b, Larch6 **_et_** _a1_ 1980). This latter term is not defined in most papers dealing with structure; ‘bicontinuous’ means that there exists a continuous path completely included in the two solvents and extending over macroscopic distances. Bicontinuity at lower water content is easily proved by simple conductimetric measurements; for L, microemulsions, more sophisticated techniques like pulsed field gradient spin-echo N M R are needed. Construction of a quantitative model of the relative distribution of water and oil is the central problem of the ‘structure of microemulsions’. This description should be ordered on a microscopic scale and disordered on a macroscopic scale. 

**A** critical discussion about the concentration range where a spherical droplet model breaks down is due to Kaler **_et_** _a1_ (1983a, b) and, as an alternative, the Talmon-Prager model using randomly filled Voronoi cells is proposed. In this work, however, the 

348 **_Y_** _Chevalier and T_ **_Zemb_** 

correlation peak in the scattering was missed because of the linear collimation used in the x-ray camera. Many and various results clearly show that the simple CRC or droplet model cannot be reconciled with experimental measurements: these are lines of isoconductivity and isoviscosity in the **L2** microemulsion phase diagram (Rushforth **_e?_** ai 1986), similar and apparently paradoxical conductivity behaviours (Georges _et a1_ 1987) could also only be interpreted through a sphere-to-cylinder or sphere-to-lamella transition (Singh _et a1_ 1983). Also, in the case of oil-in-water microemulsions, fluorescence studies could not be reconciled with spherical droplets of constant radius (Kano _e? al_ 1984) and molar volumes measurements lead to the same conclusion (Roux _er_ al1981). None of these observations can be reconciled with the occurrence of dispersed droplets, but they are also in opposition to CRC models or Talmon-Prager models: the only structural model allowing complex conductivity behaviour is the DOC model. 

The experimental problem is that the scattering curves can give ‘reasonable fits’ by any model of interacting oblate ellipsoids, even in the case where there should be some continuity in water domains as indicated by electrical conductivity (as in Caponetti **_et_** _a1_ (1986)). The only way to discriminate between models is to measure precisely the volume of the three pseudo-phases and also take into account the value of the total interfacial area: the plot of the maximum of the scattering against volume fraction is the most critical test of any structural model because of topological constraints. This type of plot has been extensively used to show that the model of spherical droplets has to break down at high concentration (Auvray _et a1_ 1984a, b, De Geyer 1987, Abillon _et al_ 1988, Zemb _e? al_ 1987). 

Microstructure is intimately related to the phase diagram: a dispersion of droplets can always be diluted by adding a mixture which has the same composition as the continuous phase. But connected lamellae or cylinders cannot be diluted without microstructural change: therefore, for this type of structure, the monophasic domain is restricted to the centre of the phase diagram and is not connected to the edges (Friberg and Buraszenka 1978). This crucial observation has often been overlooked. 

Geometrical packing constraints forbid a structure in droplets of water or oil in the reverse solvent for purely geometrical reasons in a large area of the phase diagram (Biais _et_ **_a1_** 1981, Israelachvili 1985). In regions of high surfactant content or near a two-phase boundary, the structure is unknown and there is no simple model of it, since the conductivity varies in some complex way: one observes increases and decreases of the conductivity by varying water content (Rushforth _et a1_ 1986). The first observation that conductivity does not increase as water is added was due to Schulman and Riley (1948) who called these samples ‘anomalous’ microemulsions. This conductivity drop has been studied in detail in the system potassium oleate/hexanol/ hexadecane/brine (Shah _et a1_ 1977); as in ternary systems, this conductivity drop by adding water is only consistent with the DOC model if one assumes a maximum bending radius for the interface (Barnes _e? al_ 1988b). 

This problem has been addressed by Clausse _et a1_ (1981, 1985, 1987a, b) and Heil _er_ **_a1_** (1982). These authors propose a general classification of all microemulsions into two broad classes: the type S class where the L, (oil-in-water) is disjoint from the Lz phase in the phase diagram and the so-called U class where it is possible to follow a continuous path from the oil corner to the water corner of the phase diagram. A very tiny chemical modification **of** the cosurfactant is needed to switch from a U-type phase diagram to an S-type phase diagram. There is no quantitative theory of the origin of that effect, except that it has been known for a very long time that short-chain alcohols, which distribute more equally between oil and water, favour U-type structures (Ekwall 

**_The structure of micelles and microemulsions_** 

**349** 

1969, Stilbs **_e?_** _a1_ 1983b). **A** borderline case between **U-** and S-type microemulsions has been studied by Bassereau **_et a1_** (1985). 

More microscopic structural properties are no different in quaternary microemulsions than in micelles. Microwave absorption in the GHz range shows that the ‘hydration water’, i.e. the number of water molecules directly bound to ionic headgroups and adsorbed counter-ions, is also of the order of 10 molecules per ionic headgroup (Epstein **_et_** _al_ 1983). N M R relaxation studies lead to similar order parameter profiles in microemulsions to those observed in binary micelles (Soderman and Walderhaug **1986).** 

##### **7. Conclusion** 

###### **_7.1. Chemical reactivity in micellar solutions_** 

Micellar solutions have been recognised to be powerful solvents for mixing reagents that cannot be dissolved in the same solvent (Duynstee and Grunwald 1959, Menger **_et_** _a1_ 1975). With such a solvent, two reagents, one being soluble in water and the other one being soluble in apolar solvents, can be put together in a microdiphasic solution with a very large interfacial area between two media; this improves considerably reaction rates as compared with phase transfer reactions. Apart from this obvious but interesting use, it is expected that reactions occurring at an interface could be oriented by the host structure. When several chemical reaction paths are allowed (as always in chemistry), the interface structure may accelerate or inhibit some of them and, as a consequence, induce selectivity which cannot be expected from a bulk solvent. Some reactions (but only few) that do not occur in bulk solvents were shown to occur at an interface. 

Very intensive work has been done on these ideas, and it should be recognised that results are worse than expectations: induced selectivities do exist but are not large enough to be of practical interest. The origin of this partial failure lies in the fast dynamics of the structures. For compartmentalisation and orientation of reagents to be efficient, it should remain so throughout the reaction time, so that large structureinduced selectivities are expected only when reaction rates are faster than micellar dynamics (especially exchange processes, see **8** 4.1.9). On this basis successful results were obtained with fast reactions, mainly photochemical ones, and structures with slow dynamics (bilayers and vesicles). 

Microheterogeneous media are, moreover, simple models for biostructures and attempts are currently being made to mimic biological reactions (Tsuchida **_et al_** 1984). This part of the review addresses mainly general concepts; several reviews exist and the books of Fendler and Fendler (1975) and Fendler (1982) contain exhaustive bibliographies. 

**_7.1.1. The chemist’s point_** of **_view._** A chemist involved in synthesis expects reactions with good yields and preparative scale procedures, low solvent quantities and products which are easily recoverable and pure. This is not achieved by micellar solvents which solubilise low quantities, contain surfactants which are hard to remove, and which foam on vacuum evaporation. **As** the reaction proceeds, chemical composition changes and structure modifications may occur. Few preparative scale reactions involving micellar solutions are described. For use of large quantities of reagents, microemulsions are more suitable, one reagent replacing oil (Sakellariou-Fargues **_er a1_** 1982, Perez **_et_** 

**_Y_** _Chevalier and_ **_T_** _Zemb_ 

**350** 

_a1_ 1987), provided they remain monophasic all along the reaction course. Reactions are generally better carried out in diphasic media under phase transfer conditions. Phase transfer catalysts which are often added are amphiphilic compounds, so that some micelle-like structures may be the origin of the catalytic efficiency. 

Most works on reactivity are studies of mechanisms, they are performed under conditions such that interpretation is easier: low reagent concentrations (for minimal structure modification) and dilute solutions. In-line analysis is generally performed, so that no product recovery is attempted. Rate modifications are often observed with subsequent selectivity changes. They are estimated with reference to bulk solvents or solutions below the CMC, which is a problem as both aqueous and hydrocarbon solvents are present in micellar solutions. Given a chemical mechanism, three main quantities influence reaction rates: the concentrations of reagents at the reaction site, the height of the energy barrier for reaction to occur (activation energy) and the diffusion rate of reagents. When the activation energy is low, reactions are diffusion controlled (photochemical or acid-base ones), while most organic reactions are slow and controlled by the activation energy. 

**A** typical local concentration change by micelle intervention comes from the electrostatic potential around the micelles when ionic reagents are present. Reactions of micelle-solubilised hydrophobic reagents with reactive ions are accelerated when the ion and micelle charges are opposite because of electrostatic attraction (local high concentrations); when charges are of the same sign, reaction is slowed down (Duynstee and Grunwald 1959). Quantitative explanations are possible with Poisson-Boltzmann calculations of local concentrations (Chevalier and Chachaty 1985, Bunton and Moffatt 1985). In such cases, the reaction mechanism remains the same as in bulk solvents. Cases of failure of electrostatics-based interpretation are then of greater interest since new mechanisms are involved (Gonsalves _et a1_ 1985, Bunton and Cuenca 1987). **An** effort to separate trivial concentration effects and true structure-induced mechanism modifications is on hand (Romsted 1985). 

Apart from electrostatics, local medium (solvent) effects are called forth but further analysis is prevented by the poor basic knowledge of solvent effects on chemical reactions and because interface physical properties cannot be related to any equivalent bulk solvent. The solvent effect is often a lowering of activation energy, but nothing is stated about the structural origin of this lowering. Generally speaking, it is difficult to understand chemistry in heterogeneous media without basic information about the homogeneous homologue reaction, especially in water (Rideout and Breslow 1980, Lubineau 1986). 

Structure-induced changes in diffusion of species are important when reagents are confined in small structures (micelles or microemulsion droplets): fast reaction occurs between species solubilised in the same micelle whereas diffusion across the solvent or through collision of micelles for solubilisate exchange is necessary for further reaction (Fletcher _et al_ 1982, Brochette _et a1_ 1987). Confinement in small droplets makes the encounter probability of molecules larger and accelerates diffusion controlled reactions (Gratzel 1987). **A** dimensionality effect is expected when reactions occur at an interface (two dimensional) for which diffusion is very fast and encounter probabilities high (Hatlee _et a1_ 1980, Astumian and Chock 1985). 

_7.1.2. Thephysicist’spoinr of view._ The main question of interest is: what is the relation between reactivity and structure in microheterogeneous media? The role of the physicist is to rationalise the chemist’s interpretation (based on macroscopic thermodynamic 

_The siructure of micelles and microemulsions_ 

**35** 1 

quantities) on structural grounds (Zana 1986). The rich polymorphism of structures (spatial as well as dynamic) should provide a means for controlling reactivity at will upon external medium changes (Friberg _er_ al 1973, Ramesh and Labes 1986). More than pictorial descriptions of ‘empty’ (without reactive species) and time-averaged solution structures, structural influences on diffusion and intermolecular forces on different time and spatial scales seem to be the basic concepts that chemists need for choosing appropriate reaction media. Of course, here also, structural information is not the only information needed to understand experimental results; the phase boundaries are also set by delicate energetic considerations (see as an example Gutrin and Bellocq (1988) or as reviews Roux and Coulon (1986) or Kahlweit _et a1_ (1988)). 

_7.1.3. Some examples._ The influence of structure on competition between two reaction paths is well illustrated by fluorescence quantum yield enhancement of molecules dissolved in micelles (Humphry-Baker _et a1_ 1980). This is a monolecular reaction. **A** molecule in its singlet excited state recovers its ground state via photon re-emission (fluorescence) or non-radiative transitions, energy is then transferred to the molecule and its surroundings through heat (vibrational energy). The fluorescence quantum yield is related to the relative rates of these two processes. In a micellar solution, quantum yield enhancement is observed, which corresponds to a reduction of the rate of non-radiative transitions to the ground state. Micellar influence is to squeeze the fluorescent molecule in such a way that its vibrational abilities are reduced, re-emission of a fluorescence photon is then preferred. This picture is consistent with the dependence of quantum yield on viscosity in bulk solvents (Mialocq 1982). 

The stabilisation of radical molecules by micelles is a good example of reaction inhibition by electrostatic effects on dimolecular reactions (Chevalier et _al_ 1984, Lerebours _et_ al 1985, Pileni _et_ aZ1985b). As a dicationic molecule bearing hydrophobic chains (dialkylviologen) is reduced in water by an electron donor, it gets monocharged and becomes able to enter a cationic micelle. If the electron donor is cationic too, the recombination of the two parent radicals is prevented by an electrostatic barrier. The lifetime of the radical is then increased from 2.5 ms to some 150 ms, and the back reaction becomes first order instead of second order without micelles, which suggests that the rate-controlling back reaction step is the micelle-to-water exchange of the trapped radical. Radical stabilisation by such charge separation is a key for the use **_of_** light for energy production by photochemical means (GrHtzel 1980, 1981). 

Classical organic reactions are generally slower than photochemical ones, the influence of loose aggregates such as micelles or microemulsions is thus small. They are, moreover, mainly controlled by activation energy barriers; diffusion or compartmentation of species have little importance. For such reactions, vesicles are preferred because of their slower dynamics. **_A_** fine illustration **_of_** the favourable intervention of confinement on an interface is the spontaneous polymerisation of esters of alkylglycine as vesicles which does not occur in bulk solvents (Folda _et a1_ 1982). Spontaneous polyamide formation could also be performed in reverse micelles (Armstrong _et a1_ 1978). Such reactions are of interest since a biodegradable polypeptide of controlled morphology is built up. 

##### **_7.2. Relation_** _between solubilising power and structure_ 

The influence of solubilisates on structure was discussed in §§ 5 and 6. This section deals with the influence of structure on solubilisation. The practical limitation of the 

**352** _Y Chevalier_ **_and_** _T Zemb_ 

use of micellar solvents for chemical reactivity control is due in part to the poor solubilising power of micelles. Solubilisation properties are, moreover, of importance in detergency and related applications. We restrict ourselves here to water-insoluble solubilisates, addressing only true micellar solubilisation, for which micelles are necessary for effective solubilisation (solubilisation only occurs when surfactant concentration is above the CMC, i.e. the solute does not promote micelle formation (Stearns _er al_ 1947)). In case of non-negligible solubility in water, as with short-chain alcohols, a partition between micelles and water occurs which obscures the interpretation. Water-insoluble hydrophobic molecules may solubilise either in the micellar core or in the interfacial region (Abuin _et a1_ 1984). 

For in-core solubilisation, the solubility follows linearly the surfactant concentration, so that solubilising power can be defined as the amount of solubilate per surfactant molecule. The general result is then a lower solubilising power of micellar cores as compared with bulk alkanes (Elworthy _et a1_ 1968). If swollen micelles are modelled as hydrocarbon droplets separated from water by a curved surface of tension, a Laplace pressure _P_ occurs inside the droplet because of curvature R _( P_ = _y /_ R, _y_ being the interfacial tension), which reduces the solubility of hydrocarbons (Wishnia 1963). This explanation works very well (Mukerjee 1979, 1980) but is phenomenological: it does not inform us about the physical origin of micellar solubilisation. 

The curvature radius is indeed that of the swollen micelle, not an intrinsic property of the surfactant or solute molecule. When solute is incorporated into micelles, it can fill the centre of the micellar core, so that surfactant molecules get more freedom in conformation (surfactant methyl groups do not have to be present at the micelle centre), the micellar radius can thus exceed the length of a fully extended chain _1,,_ and micelles can grow without deformation. **In** other words, a solute-free micelle is a frustrated system, solute introduction releases the frustration of packing at constant internal density and a swollen micelle should be more stable. The packing criterion _a,l,/u_ no longer applies. Swollen micelles are indeed larger than solute-free ones (Almgren and Swarup 1982). 

Solubilisation is then limited by the curvature of the swollen aggregate: when the area per headgroup has reached its ‘natural’ value, surfactant coverage is optimum and no more solubilisation is possible. The relation between solubilising ability and structure is then simple: it is governed by the optimal curvature (or area per headgroup _ao)_ of the surfactant film at a hydrocarbon-water interface; the lower this curvature, the larger the solubilisation. Experiments show this trend: long-chain or double-chain surfactants solubilise more hydrocarbon (even if the solubilising power is defined as the solubilisation per surfactant methylene) (McBain and Johnson 1944, Heller and Klevens 1946, Kolthoff and Stricks 1948, Mukerjee 1979, Shinoda and Sagitani 1983), large micelles (with low _a,)_ are more efficient than spherical ones (Brown and Nauman 1967, Robins and Thomas 1968, Ozeki and Ikeda 1985, Imae **_et_** _a1_ 1986, Abe **_et_** _a1_ 1987), salt addition in ionic micellar solutions which decreases _a,,_ increases the solubilising power (McBain and Johnson 1944, McBain and Green 1946, Venable and Nauman 1964), the solubisation ability of non-ionic alkylpolyoxyethylene ethers follows the hydrophobicity (related to _a,)_ of their headgroups (Nakagawa 1966). 

For solubilisation to increase further, a fourth component is added, which solubilises at the interface: short-chain alcohols then give way to microemulsions. Very large solubilising powers are obtained with microemulsions in which the cosurfactant is able to adjust _a,_ to the aggregate curvature (see **0** 6). For molecules which solubilise at the interface (long-chain alcohols, aromatic hydrocarbons (Eriksson and Gillberg 1966, 

_The structure of micelles and microemulsions_ 

353 

Johansson _et a1_ 1976, Samori and Mattivi 1986), hydrophobic dyes (Ganesh _et a1_ **1982,** 1984)), larger solubilisations are then generally obtained. The curvature reduction is easily shown by a transition to elongated micelles (Henriksson _er a1_ 1977b, Eriksson _er a1_ 1982) or lamellar mesophases (Robins and Thomas 1968, Ekwall _et a1_ 1969b) as solute is added. Interesting synergism effects of benzene-cyclohexane or methyl methacrylate-hexane solute mixtures were obtained in this way (Ciiceres and Lissi 1984, Nagarajan and Ruckenstein 1984, Nagarajan _et a1_ 1984, Chaiko _et a1_ 1984). 

##### **_7.3._** _Some controversial structures_ 

We have somewhat arbitrarily eliminated all structures presenting a crystalline longrange order as lyotropic liquid crystals. Cubic phases are usually very stiff and show a large number of crystalline reflection orders and can therefore be unambiguously detected by diffraction experiments. The lamellar and hexagonal phases have an optical anisotropy which is easily observed between crossed polarisers. The class of lyotropic nematic phases is borderline and they could be classified in either of the two categories: microemulsions or liquid crystals. It has been noticed that there should be structural relations between lyotropic liquid crystals and microemulsions. When their chemical compositions are close, the first Bragg reflection of a liquid crystal occurs at the same angle as the maximum of the broad peak characteristic of microemulsions (Fontell _et_ **_a1_** 1983). However, one should be aware that a systematic relation between the ordered structure of liquid crystalline phases and the liquid one of adjacent isotropic solutions does not exist (see **3** 4.1.3). 

The transition between micelles or microemulsions (dilute ‘gas’ or concentrated ‘liquid’ state) and the more ordered phases (solid at least in one direction) occurs through a well defined phase transition. Second-order phase transitions can be expected from phase diagrams, but have not yet been shown in surfactant systems. Very slow phase separations are difficult to distinguish from new types of liquid-liquid equilibria with very different structures, as opposed to critical fluctuations. In the very dilute microemulsions made of toluene, brine, butanol and less than 0.1% of SDS, the low interfacial area available induces very large characteristic sizes in surfactant aggregates. The typical length in those systems is 100 nm, as revealed by the yellow to red colours of the samples. If the basic structure were spheres, one would have only very dilute droplets. This work shows that not only lamellar phases, but also microemulsions can be swelled by dilution. Moreover, very thick interfaces, in the millimetre range, of unknown structure appear in that system (Gambi _er a1_ 1987a, b). 

The term liquid crystalline microemulsion or birefringent microemulsion, sometimes used in the past, should no longer be used, because this nomenclature hides the fact that these phases are identical to the classical lamellar phases when they are swollen by large amounts of oil or water. 

The emerging picture of the very large number of structural studies of optically isotropic systems is that simple models of interacting spheres hold surprisingly well in the dilute region. Spherical droplets are very loose, fluctuating, with fast molecular exchange processes. Interactions are mainly excluded volume effects and either a long-range screened electrostatic potential for direct ionic micelles, or a short-range attractive one for non-ionic and/or reverse systems. In the concentrated regime, the DOC model is currently the only proposed structure compatible with the peak position in scattering patterns, but alternative descriptive models of bicontinuous materials could probably work. 

**354** **_Y Chevalier and_** _T_ **_Zemb_** 

The main point is that one phase, defined as a monophasic area in a phase diagram, does not correspond in surfactant systems to one single type of structure: cylinders can gradually transform into coalescing spheres or lamellae of unilamellar vesicles can, at some temperature, emerge from a solution of micelles (Gershfeld _et_ **_a1_ 1986)** without leaving this monophasic area. It is now well established that micelles are in equilibrium with surfactant as a molecular dispersion in the solvent. It is not yet firmly established whether micelles of a pure compound can also dynamically coexist with unilamellar vesicles or if first reports about it are due to impurities (Brady **_et_** _a1_ **1984).** However, the usual dispersions of bilayers called ‘vesicles’ are prepared by sonication and correspond to a kinetic stability: the corresponding point in a phase diagram belongs to a lamellar phase. The scattering spectra are close to spectra obtained in microemulsions and can be understood using similar methods as for micellar systems (Muddle er **_al_ 1983).** 

In the near future, the structure of the ‘anomalous’ isotropic phases called L3 in phase diagrams (figure **23)** has also to be elucidated, together with the mechanism of the viscosity ‘accidents’ occurring close to lamellar phases in ordinary direct micellar solutions (Bellocq and Roux **1987)** (figure **38).** Also some strange scattering spectra of large structures have been observed but the phase diagram of this system is not known (Tabony **_et_** _a1_ 1987). Some new types of foams, disordered cylinders with large periodicity **(100** nm), predicted by the **_DOC_** model, remain to be quantitatively studied. 

This continuity in structural change within one ’phase’ of the diagram has been identified as a key point for progress in surfactant structures by Shinoda **(1985),** Ninham and Evans **(1986)** and Evans and Ninham **(1986).** For instance, it is now widely accepted that there is no difference in nature between emulsions and microemulsions. **A** solution is called an emulsion when it is opaque, due to a very strong scattering of light: the characteristic size of oil and water domains is at least one order of magnitude higher than in microemulsions. Emulsions which cannot be broken appear frequently in the vicinity of a microemulsion domain in phase diagrams (Fontell **_er_** _a1_ **1986).** In the ternary system **nonylphenol-9-polyoxyethylene/water/cyclohexanone,** spon-

**Figure 39.** Small-angle neutron scattering spectrum of a spontaneous ternary emulsion (DDAB/water/dodecane): two reflection orders are superimposed to a very strong zeroangle scattering. This type of scattering is not observed with micelles, nor with a dispersion of lamellar microcrystallites. 

taneous emulsion and microemulsion coexist within the same ‘single-phase’ region of the phase diagram. The opaque emulsion region is then formally distinguished from the microemulsion by partial molecular volumes. No theory of microemulsion exists which can predict the appearance of a disordered microemulsion state near the liquid crystalline phase. Therefore, it is not known whether the kinetic stability of emulsions involves the same or a different set of molecular interactions. Typically small-angle scattering spectra of emulsions are very different from those of microemulsions (figure 39). Whether or not structures are retained upon cooling is still studied: the ‘gel-microemulsion’ transition involves complete modification of x-ray scattering (Nimtz **_et a1_** 1986). **At** very high cooling rates, electron microscopy has been used: droplet-like structures have been observed. Optical diffractograms of the transmission electron micrograph pictures are similar to common small-angle scattering data (Dubochet et _a1_ 1984). 

The key to the understanding of the occurrence of different microstructures in a single macroscopic ‘phase’ in a composition diagram is the relation between molecular properties and aggregation phenomena. Indeed, the elementary ‘particle’ in colloidal physics is a flexible molecule or an aggregate. Up to now, the interfacial curvature energy, the electrostatic energy averaged over few molecular distances and the water-tooil transfer energies have received most attention in theoretical work. The lowest possible approximation level is given by the molecular shape parameter _a&/_ **_1)._ A** more refined general framework has recently been published (Overbeek **_et_** _a1_ 1987) and the predictions remain to be tested. **As** was expressed by Ninham and Evans (1986), the relation between geometrical constraints due to steric hindrance in molecular packing and the statistical mechanics of disordered interfaces in heterogeneous systems is the major challenge to a theory offering some predictive power of microemulsion stability.
